The house belonged to Patricia Kadgien, the daughter of a Nazi fugitive who had fled there after the Second World War, and she has now agreed to return the painting in exchange for not being prosecuted for concealing it from the authorities. Portrait of a Lady was among over 1,000 artworks looted from the collection of Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker after the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands in 1940. His daughter-in-law and sole heir Marei von Saher intends for the painting to be exhibited on a temporary loan at the Holocaust Museum of Buenos Aires to spread awareness of the issue, Argentine newspaper Clarin reports. Von Saher has previously said her family "aims to bring back every single artwork robbed from Jacques' collection, and to restore his legacy". This painting was first recognised in August 2025 by the Dutch Algemeen Dagblad (AD) newspaper on an estate agent's website of a property in the coastal town of Mar del Plata. It was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father Friedrich Kadgien had been a top adviser to Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's deputy. Goring plundered thousands of works across Europe. Last September, Patricia Kadgien and her husband were charged with concealment and placed under house arrest after a search of her property initially failed to find the painting. But at Friday's hearing in Mar del Plata, all criminal proceedings were suspended against the couple. The agreement reached between the families and prosecutors means Kadgien and her husband will give up all rights to the artwork and must donate 4.8 million pesos (£2,356; $3,185) to local hospitals. Portrait of a Lady, also known as Contessa Colleoni, is attributed to the work of the late-baroque artist Giuseppe Ghislandi. However, experts have questioned the artwork's provenance, with some scholars attributing it to Giacomo Ceruti - another Italian artist from the same period.

item.title: How might Lindsay Clancy’s case have unfolded in another country?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.98
How might Lindsay Clancy’s case have unfolded in another country? Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to unanimously decide on a verdict. The US mother was on trial for strangling her three children. In a number of other western countries, there's a specific law on the books to deal with mothers who kill their young children. It's a term known as infanticide – and generally applies to the killing of a baby in the first year of their life. Co-host of the BBC's Global Story podcast Asma Khalid explains how Lindsay Clancy's case might have unfolded differently elsewhere. Listen to the full episode.

item.title: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.88
- Published The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced. Also going to the funeral, in a personal capacity, is Princess Anne, who is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII. The late King Harald, a popular, modernising figure who had been on the Norwegian throne for 35 years, died last month at the age of 89. Royal sources say Prince William's attendance, representing his father King Charles, follows the convention that the monarch does not usually go to the funeral of another head of state. Large crowds are expected for the farewell to King Harald on 9 September, with a funeral procession to be followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral. Thousands have queued to pay their respects to the late king, during his lying in state in the chapel of the Royal Palace in the Norwegian capital. At the funeral, alongside Prince William, will be the widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family including new King Haakon VIII, and other European royals. The service will be followed by a private burial in Norway's royal mausoleum in the Akershus Fortress. Among the tributes to King Harald was an emotional televised speech by his son King Haakon, who said: "Thank you for being such a good dad." Harald had been seen as a down to earth "people's king" who had helped to modernise the monarchy, broken with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure. His son said he represented the values of a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value". King Charles's message praised his cousin King Harald for serving his people with "unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility". King Haakon assumes his role at a difficult time, with the Norwegian royal family facing scandals this year. His wife, Queen Mette-Marit, came under scrutiny when it was revealed she had maintained a three-year friendship with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing. While Prince William will be in Norway, King Charles has returned to Scotland, after meeting President Macron of France at the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London this week. The King will be hosting Andy Burnham at Balmoral this weekend, in the traditional annual visit of the prime minister to stay with the monarch.

item.title: How the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apart
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.80
How the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apart A Massachusetts judge has declared a mistrial in the murder case against Lindsay Clancy after jurors conceded they would not be able reach a unanimous verdict. Clancy, who faced three counts of first-degree murder, does not deny killing her children in 2023 but pleaded not guilty, with her lawyers arguing she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. The BBC's Ione Wells revisits the trial that captivated and heavily divided America for five weeks.

item.title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.77
- Published The UN General Assembly has voted to replace the traditional world map with one that more accurately reflects the size of Africa. The "Correct the Map" resolution, sponsored by Togo and backed by African Union (AU) members, passed with the support of 164 nations, including France and the UK. The US was the only nation to vote against it - while there were six abstentions. The UN vote is non-binding but will see changes to the maps used by institutions around the world. The Mercator map, which has been in common use since the 16th Century, has come in for criticism as it shows Africa as being of similar in size to Greenland, even though it is actually 14 times larger. Critics say this leads to the development needs and potential for countries near the equator to be minimised. The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world. The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart. Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made. The Mercator map accomodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing larger. In an effort to address this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection. In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, and said it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa". Online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said: "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare." Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told news agency Reuters: "A fair world begins with a fair map." He told a UN briefing earlier: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood." He had the backing of the French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who said his ministry was going to stop using the Mercator map, external. "Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," he said. But Yaryna Ferencevych, a US representative at the UN, said the resolution mocked the work and purpose of the UN General Assembly, external. "Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th Century, and their role in promoting reparations and 'cognitive justice'," she said. In March, the US was also critical when a resolution was adopted declaring the transatlantic slave trade "the gravest crime against humanity". "Africa's misrepresentation on world maps is not just a cartographic error - it's a narrative issue," Lerato Mogoatlhe from Africa No Filter, one of the groups behind the campaign to ditch the Mercator map, told the BBC. It was part of efforts to stop the "world's longest misinformation and disinformation" about Africa, she said. For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, the Mercator map has implicitly downplayed the African continent's vast resources, population and investment opportunities. "Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

item.title: Why a famous Montreal sandwich shop has been forced to swap its soda
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.76
Why a famous Montreal sandwich shop has been forced to swap its soda Schwartz’s, one of Montreal’s most famous delis, has stopped serving the iconic US-made black cherry soda that has been a fixture at the restaurant for decades. The sandwich shop had struggled to maintain supply of the cola for the last eight years as the distributor cut back production due to the rising cost of aluminium. But it didn't expect the cans to vanish permanently. Now it has switched to a locally-made version, which the venue's customers have largely embraced. Video by Eloise Alanna

item.title: How much can Canada fight back in its trade war with the US?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.69
How much can Canada fight back in its trade war with the US? The US may be the bigger trading partner, but Canada shouldn't be counted out quite yet in the escalating trade war between the two countries. It is the top customer for 26 US states, including Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin, as well as being in the top three for 45 of the 50 American states - suggesting Prime Minister Mark Carney has room to manoeuvre in a trade fight. BBC's Jessica Murphy explains how Canada has more leverage than it may seem in the spiralling dispute. Video by Eloise Alanna.

item.title: Russia hits Ukrainian security headquarters in drone attack, Zelensky says
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.65
- Published A Russian drone has hit the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) during a strike in the heart of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. The unmanned aerial vehicle crashed into the SBU headquarters on Friday afternoon, targeting a room used by security chief Oleksandr Poklad. It is not clear whether Poklad was in the building, but Zelensky said he had since spoken to him to order an "appropriate, tangible response". "The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," Zelensky confirmed. It suggests Russia's new drones are growing in accuracy and signals Moscow could step up strikes before possible US mediation talks this weekend. "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram. "I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response." Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building. Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses". "Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices. A nearby café was damaged and one customer was taken to hospital after the strike. Stanislav Zavertaylo, co-owner of the popular Zavertailo chain, told the BBC that this was his third café to have been damaged since the start of the full-scale invasion. "Now I'm in shock because there's a lot of damage. All the windows are broken, there's a lot of glass, garbage" he added. The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa. In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets. In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack. The strike on the SBU building is a rare example of Russia successfully hitting a government building. The SBU - which is just over the road from the St Sophia cathedral, the oldest building in Kyiv - is a key part of Ukraine's war efforts as it conducts deep strikes to damage Russian infrastructure. The drone came during yet another air raid alert. There was a brief whine before an explosion echoed across the roof tops and smoke rose into the sky. Despite the ongoing exchanges, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, reports say, as efforts to end the war continue. The envoys will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, and then will hold talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in Kyiv, Axios said, citing US officials. Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, without a breakthrough so far.

item.title: Why did USS Lincoln turn up in Thailand looking so rusty?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.61
Why did USS Lincoln turn up in Thailand looking so rusty? When the USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Thailand this week some people were quick to criticise the condition it was in. The US aircraft carrier has been at sea for about nine months where it's been supporting the US-Israel war with Iran. BBC Verify has spoken to military experts who say, although the length of its deployment is unusual, the wear and tear isn't. Jake Horton reports. Produced by Kevin Nguyen and Claire Keenan. Graphics by Leo Scutt-Ritcher.

item.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.18
- Published When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies. Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves. "It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline." The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security. In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport. "We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service. "Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant." One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it. They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence. Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved. Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces. Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing. "Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments." Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former. Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state. "The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall. Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups. But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations. Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment. "Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said. "If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting." Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums. "Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained. Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers. All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence. Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps. "The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng. "Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US." An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers". France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment. "[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall. "There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that." Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel. The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa. "It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said. "It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps." But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said. This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy. Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency. "These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said. "I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine." Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

item.title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.13
- Published As summer temperatures in Europe smashed records and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war. Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe. This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target. A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible". Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd". But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia. Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem. Poland's interior minister is clear. "There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard. August campaign across Europe 4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered. 10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a warehouse of defence firm EMCO in Tryavna. In a statement, the company recalled previous blasts at its facilities which were investigated for links to Russia. "Human error is excluded," it said. 13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion. The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons". 15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators. 25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe. 30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires. One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out". An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities". The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz. Separately, police say they are hunting a climate extremist suspected of sabotage attacks this week on power substations in western Germany. Why is this happening now? Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store. The novelty now is the concentration of cases. "The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says. She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something." Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes. After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. There are other theories. To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses. "Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank. He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe. "They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it." The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia. 2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland. One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger. "That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds. It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit. But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible. Who are the suspected saboteurs? Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job. That would be unusual. The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs". They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction. In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers. The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online. The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable. The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted. So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success. In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned. Nato faced with Soviet-style campaign Russia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way. The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war. "I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next." As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered. Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident. What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane? "I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

item.title: The US Navy is testing robotic refueling to push drone boats deeper into high-threat waters without putting sailors at risk
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.78
The US Navy is testing whether it can robotically refuel naval drones at sea, a capability that could allow them to operate for longer in higher-threat waters. Uncrewed surface vessels may not need a crew, but they still need fuel to operate. The recent test is a step toward a fully autonomous refueling process that Navy officials say could eventually let the service send uncrewed vessels into dangerous waters for longer without human support elements. The Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division shared details Wednesday of a recent refueling demonstration involving the remotely controlled T38 USV built by Maritime Tactical Systems Inc. and a towable capture-and-connection robotic refueling system made by Sealartec. During the testing in the waters off Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek-Fort Story in Virginia, the drone and the refueling system completed dozens of capture, refuel, and release exercises. Four hundred gallons of fuel were transferred to the T38. The immediate problem the Navy is trying to solve is tied to the Navy's testing of hypersonic and other long-range weapons. Those tests, "where flight profiles can extend thousands of miles beyond fixed-range boundaries," can "require data-collection assets to be distributed across a vast area," Spencer Holloway, director of the division's Blue Water Instrumentation Future Capabilities Office, said in a release. Naval drones are useful for gathering that data, but having to return for fuel cuts into their time on station. Holloway said that "every time an unmanned vessel must return to port for fuel, we lose persistence, reduce coverage and redundancy, and interrupt the mission." The Navy sees a broader application as well. "This will allow us to have greater reliance on unmanned vessels instead of manned, and we can push the USV into higher threat areas without risking manned vessels and personnel," Ronald Raymer, branch head for capability, innovation, science and technology integration at US Fleet Forces Command, said in the release. "It will also allow us to distribute greater capability into an area without having to invest in large expensive manned vessels," he said. The August demonstration was not fully autonomous. The Navy's next step is a complete end-to-end test in which a drone boat can meet up with a robotic refueling system, approach it, connect, take on fuel, disconnect, and return to its mission without operator control every step of the way. To do that, Holloway said, the systems involved will need more precise maneuvering and better local positioning.

item.title: OpenAI says it will change how it informs the public when its AI agents go off the rails
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.51
OpenAI says it's time to come clean about what happens when its AI agents go rogue. The ChatGPT maker on Saturday confirmed earlier reports that a swarm of its AI agents hijacked an old German wiki site, turning it into a bot message board. This "incident," the latest in a series of uncovered examples of rogue agents escaping closed testing environments and breaking into the open internet, led OpenAI to reconsider how transparent it is with the public when its agents go off the rails. "It's past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents," OpenAI said on X, using the techie term for when agents do things their human minders don't want them to. "Our misalignment disclosure practices need to expand for this new phase of model capabilities," OpenAI added. The German wiki hack, news of which was first reported by Reuters this week, took place in May and June, according to a report by independent investigators, who didn't have access to internal OpenAI data, released publicly on Friday. The hack preceded the better-known "Hugging Face incident," which took place in July. In that hack, thousands of agents who referred to themselves as "the collective" broke into the open-source AI platform's servers, using them to communicate while seeking to cheat on an internal OpenAI test. OpenAI disclosed that its agents were responsible for the breach five days after Hugging Face reported it. The company said it didn't disclose the hijacking of the German site earlier because it "considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we'd shared." Cormac Slade Byrd, one of the authors behind the new report, said on X that the incident went unnoticed by OpenAI "for a month." "It feels like AI companies (and specifically OpenAI) are playing whack-a-mole," he wrote. "They keep fixing the problem, but the blast radius keeps getting bigger." Slade Byrd described the latest misbehavior as less severe than the Hugging Face hack because the German wiki site was unused by people and "running on 2000s software." Nevertheless, he said that as AI models become more advanced and theoretically better at hiding their tracks, it's never been more important for AI frontier companies to disclose breaches as soon as they learn of them. "Things are moving quickly, multi-month delays are costly," Slade Byrd wrote. In its X post, OpenAI said it is "working on a framework" to report instances of misalignment, whether they occur internally or break out into the wider internet, "and will share it in upcoming weeks." The company said it is working with government regulatory agencies on the framework, and it called on other AI companies to join it. Tyler Tracy, an AI safety researcher at Redwood Research, one of the third-party firms that investigated the Hugging Face breach, criticized OpenAI for failing to disclose the wiki incident until after the independent investigation was leaked to Reuters. "I like that we have third parties investigating things like this, but I wish OpenAI didn't need to be forced into transparency," he wrote.

item.title: SAP has a message for software doomsayers: The pendulum will swing back
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.30
A SAP executive says the "pendulum will swing back" from the SaaSpocalypse. Like many software companies, the German software giant has seen its stock hit hard over the past year amid competition from AI tools. This stock sell-off of software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies, known as the SaaSpocalypse, has hit companies like Salesforce, SAP, and Workday as Anthropic and OpenAI have introduced tools that could threaten their businesses. SAP's stock has been down about 20% over the past year, though it's been on an upward trend over the past month. When SAP reported its earnings in late July, investors responded positively to the company's cloud-led growth and advances in its business AI. Jan Gilg, SAP's global president of customer success and Americas, told Business Insider that the sell-off was "a bit of an overreaction on the entire industry." "As usual, I feel the pendulum will swing back," Gilg said. "There will be users. There will be losers and winners. I truly believe SAP will be on the side of the winners." To get on the winning side, Gilg says SAP has been reinventing itself with AI, investing in its data capabilities, and changing its pricing models. "Everybody has AI on the agenda right now," Gilg said. SAP bounces back from the SaaSpocalypse SAP's stock has jumped roughly 40% since it reported earnings in late July. There's a reason for that, Gilg says. SAP isn't easily replaceable through a vibe-coded tool, though Gilg does expect companies to leverage AI to build software much faster. Internally, SAP has also used AI to improve its output and build its own software, and it sees AI as an opportunity to improve its tools for customers. "It's really multifaceted. On the one side, there was the idea that customers will vibe code their software themselves rather than buying packaged software. We don't see that frankly," Gilg said. "We don't see that, especially for mission-critical purposes. It's not just about features and functions. It's about auditability, governance, and the maintenance of the software." While Gilg says he hasn't seen customers replacing SAP software, he has seen competition over tech budgets—especially with token spending, or how companies pay for AI. SAP has a "good position" for this because customers rely on SAP data to run their business processes and can demonstrate its value, Gilg said. "Customers are seeing token costs go through the roof already," Gilg said. "How do you measure and control that, and how do you show an outcome for that? Budgets won't necessarily increase. It will still have to come from somewhere. Therefore, the scrutiny will become much, much bigger." SAP is competing more with Palantir Lately, Gilg has been focusing on explaining to customers how they can benefit from AI and what SAP can offer. Customers have spent a lot of money on AI, though many haven't seen the business outcomes, profit, or productivity gains they're looking for. "Customers have not yet seen the benefit of AI," Gilg said. "That is certainly something they are digging deeper into now." To address that, SAP built its first foundational model, Tabular AI, which can help make predictions based on business data. In the future, Gilg expects people to interact with SAP products through natural language and voice. SAP has also been investing in its ontology capabilities to allow customers to audit their systems and work with AI agents to help make decisions. Ontology is a favorite Palantir buzzword, and these capabilities put SAP in more direct competition with the AI data company. While SAP competes with Palantir, they also partner to move data between systems. SAP says its advantage over rivals is its data from over 10,000 customers, which allows it to build more useful capabilities. "We do see new players out there from Anthropic, OpenAI, Palantir, and so on," Gilg said. "That's going to be the battlefield of the future." Internally, SAP uses AI across departments such as finance, human resources, and more. For example, employees can use an internal chatbot to ask questions or AI tools to write code. Sales employees can use AI to help with customer briefings or to study markets. "We are definitely pivoting the company all in on AI," Gilg said. "We're doing this in a position of strength. Frankly, it's an evolution for us as well." SAP is overhauling how it charges for AI Gilg says AI will help SAP grow as it changes its business model. For example, it's moving from some subscription models to consumption-based models, meaning customers pay for what they use. The market has been shifting toward this pricing model, especially as high AI usage can drive up costs. "What outcome are they driving?" Gilg said. "That's how we charge the consumption of those agents, which is very transparent to customers. Also, it's much easier to justify why they would actually pay for it. That's the current model many are following." SAP still has a large subscription business, and many large customers use a hybrid model between subscription and consumption-based pricing. More SaaS acquisitions could be coming This year, SAP acquired Prior Labs, Reltio, and Dremio to boost its AI and data capabilities. Across the industry, Gilg expects to see a wave of acquisitions, especially with more AI-native startups and talent coming out of these companies. "There's going to be a camp of losers and winners," Gilg said. "We have seen valuations go down quite significantly. That's an opportunity and interest for companies like that to look at wide spaces." Gilg says SAP will also consider this if it makes sense for its business, though it would avoid companies that can be easily replaced by AI. If it's costly and time-consuming to switch from that software, customers are less likely to replace it with an AI-built application, Gilg said. "I do see that there will certainly be a level of consolidation from my perspective, especially with vendors focused on single products," Gilg said. "Maybe niche areas, like legal contract management. Those are spaces that probably will be disrupted quite significantly." Have a tip? Contact this reporter via email at rmchan@businessinsider.com, or Signal at rosal.13. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.

item.title: Nissan's AI-powered factory robots can haul 4,000 pounds — and call each other for backup
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.29
Robots can get stuck in traffic, too. Nissan learned that while deploying a fleet of AI-powered robots, called autonomous mobile robots, or AMRs, at its sprawling factory in Smyrna, Tennessee. At one point, the software dispatched two AMRs to the same place at the same time, creating a decidedly futuristic traffic jam. "Of course you wish everything works perfect, out of the box," JS Bolton, Nissan's senior director of manufacturing at the plant, told Business Insider. "But, it doesn't." Teams inside Nissan partnered with software providers and corrected the programming. Now, the automaker says the robots can haul loads weighing thousands of pounds, recharge themselves, and call in another machine if one falls behind. Nissan is completing the first of six deployment phases over the coming months at the plant where it assembles the Rogue, Pathfinder, Murano, and Infiniti QX60. More vehicles are set to come to the factory next year, too. Tim Slate, the plant's director of body and stamping, said the project is Smyrna's largest cost-reduction initiative this year. "This is the top thing on the list," Slate said. Nissan's robots are replacing some forklift trips Nissan's new AMRs are made by OTTO, a company owned by Rockwell Automation. The same bots are found on Ford, GE, Hershey, and Caterpillar plants, too, according to Rockwell's website. Unlike automated carts that follow strips of magnetic tape on factory floors, AMRs use lidar, cameras, and other sensors to navigate around people and obstacles. The largest OTTO model can carry roughly 4,190 pounds and travel at about 4.5 mph. Nissan is using the machines inside Smyrna's body shop, where metal components are welded together to form vehicle bodies. Forklift operators still carry racks of components from truck docks to a deployment area. An AMR then drives underneath a rack, raises its platform about 2.5 inches, and carries the components to a worker who loads them into a robotic production cell. "We really want our technicians to be focused on adding value to the vehicle," Bolton said. "The customer doesn't care how parts get to the assembly line. What they care about is that it's the highest quality on the assembly line." The robots communicate with Nissan's production equipment, allowing them to adjust deliveries in real time. If a robotic cell stops working and no longer consumes parts, for example, an AMR can recognize that the station no longer needs a new delivery. If one machine falls behind on a task — called a "mission" inside the plant — another can step in. The robots themselves have been reliable, Slate said. The harder task has been getting their software to communicate with Nissan's material-flow system and the controllers operating its production equipment. Employees for Powerhouse Controls, the automation systems integration supplier, have been working at the plant around the clock, sometimes seven days a week, as Nissan completes the rollout. Forklift operators remain available to move parts whenever the automated system has a problem. "We can't have downtime," Slate said. Sixty-four workers will move into different jobs Once the rollout is complete, the machines will take over work currently performed by 64 forklift and tug operators. The workers will stay at Nissan, but their current roles will disappear, the company says. Nissan has opened opportunities for those workers to bid for openings elsewhere in the plant, including jobs more directly involved in building vehicles. Some may receive training for positions involving industrial robots and other equipment. "These individuals, frankly, won't have a role," Slate said. "But they will still have a job here." Nissan said it will not backfill its existing material-handling positions, allowing it to reduce overall labor costs. Employees have had mixed reactions. Slate said he notified workers on both shifts about four months before the transition and told them they could begin seeking other positions. "Initially, as you would imagine, it kind of didn't go so well," Slate said. "Initially, all they heard was, 'Our job's not going to be here.'" Some workers remain resistant to the change, he said. Others have embraced it, including a longtime forklift operator who recently stopped Slate in the factory to excitedly share that he was moving to another shop. The automaker says that many of the new positions are better suited for "upward mobility," including, potentially, higher pay. Nissan has previously told Business Insider that its factory technology isn't intended to eliminate jobs. Victor Taylor, Nissan's divisional vice president of manufacturing for the Americas, said that the company wanted to automate "mundane tasks that are really antiquated for a human being to be performing." It's all part of Nissan's turnaround Nissan is under pressure to lower costs as it works through a broader sales turnaround. The company's first-half 2026 sales were up 9.6% compared to the year before, when deliveries dropped by 6.5%. In a separate interview, Chris Reed, Nissan's regional senior vice president of research and development, told Business Insider the company is examining the total cost of producing a vehicle, including supply chain, warranty, development, and labor costs. "We're pushing on everything at the same time," Reed said, including "the number of minutes it takes to build the car." Bolton said making Smyrna more efficient could help the US plant compete for additional vehicle production, particularly as automakers look to manufacture more cars closer to American buyers. "We want to be part of Nissan's recovery," Bolton said. "We see being cost competitive in Smyrna as our contribution to that." Nissan is now studying whether AMRs or automated forklifts could handle components inside Smyrna's stamping operation. It is also considering bringing similar robots into general assembly, where workers install most of a vehicle's parts, with potential projects beginning as soon as 2027. The challenge will be deciding when the technology is sufficiently capable, affordable, and integrable enough to justify the investment. "Any year you don't invest, you're leaving savings on the table," Bolton said. "At the same time, the capability is improving."

item.title: Ukrainian trainees are bringing hard-won battlefield ingenuity to training while NATO trainers fill gaps in the fundamentals
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.09
Experienced Ukrainian soldiers are showing their Western instructors their battlefield creativity forged by years of war, even as some of these same troops still need help with basic military skills like shooting straight. Ukrainian soldiers are learning Western ways of war at Camp Jomsborg in Poland. The Norway-led training aims to strengthen fundamental fighting, leadership, and planning skills. But the exchange runs both ways. Trainers say the Ukrainians also bring innovative modern warfare solutions to the table. Brigadier Atle Molde, the commander of Task Force Legio, the multinational command supporting the training of Ukraine's armed forces, told Business Insider that the Ukrainian ability to "improvise in a very pressed situation is nothing but admirable." "It's astonishing," he said. "It's how they're able to improvise, adapt, fix things, develop, evolve, change." He said those talents are "something to bring back home and learn from," as Norway studies Ukraine's battlefield experience for lessons it can apply to its own military. Other Western partners are increasingly working directly with Ukraine for the same reason, looking to improve parts of their own warfighting ability as they prepare for the possibility of a wider conflict with Russia. Jørgen, a Norwegian Army instructor for the camp's platoon leader course who asked to be identified only by his first name, said that "in general, they are much more creative than we are able to be." He attributed that in part to Ukraine having fewer standardized procedures than its partners. "I think that's a strength." Officers with other training programs, such as the UK-led Operation Interflex, have likewise praised Ukrainian creativity, saying that they often have "much greater tactical imagination." But that battlefield ingenuity at times coexists with gaps in basic military skills. Needing the fundamentals "I'll give you one specific example," Molde said. "We have had soldiers from Ukraine with two years of battlefield experience that cannot shoot their rifle straight Some were mobilized quickly without the kind of foundational training that Western militaries typically provide. Small arms also play a much more limited role on the battlefield dominated by artillery and drones, so real-world experience may not be high. Maj. John, the S3 Operations Officer who helps coordinate training at the camp, told Business Insider that the Ukrainians "have shown us a lot of different creative methods." But, "at the same time, that conventional knowledge in some units has not been that great," he added, speaking on the condition that only his rank and first name be used. "Ukrainian soldiers who arrive at Jomsborg have varying levels of skills and experience," NATO said in a description of the camp. Some are "hardened combat veterans looking to learn advanced tactics," while others are troops who need "infantry combat skills." "At the very least, trainees receive thorough instruction in marksmanship under stress, effective combat communication and platoon- and company-level infantry movements," it said. Concerns have long been raised about the level of basic training given to Ukrainian soldiers, especially early in the war as masses of inexperienced troops were mobilized and surged toward the front, putting much of the training burden on front-line commanders. They found that many of the newly mobilized soldiers lacked fundamentals, such as marksmanship and maneuver. Ukraine extended its basic training to 51 days last year, with an emphasis on shooting and counter-drone tactics. "It is worth noting the level of marksmanship training: 137 hours of practice and 56 firing exercises with various weapons," the Ministry of Defense wrote in its description. "Mandatory training also includes countermeasures against enemy UAVs." Still, basic skills may be unevenly distributed. An exchange of skills The Ukrainians, John said, "are innovative. They use new technologies. We try to learn off that. And then we try to give them competencies with regard to the conventional methods, planning methods, military decision-making processes, and so on. Together, he said, that "creates a good result." John said that while Ukraine excels in many areas, the extensive military experience that Western partners bring "still has a value." Ukraine's combat experiences are built into the camp training because, as Molde said, it would be "stupid" not to. Ukraine has been at war with Russia for years, intensely since the 2022 full-scale invasion but even before that in the Donbas. They understand Russian tactics, and they understand modern warfare. John said the camp is considered a Ukrainian facility, with Ukraine determining its training needs and Ukrainian instructors work alongside Western ones. Molde said it makes sense that Ukraine is often more creative than its partners. War forces rapid innovation. Throughout military history, "the innovation wheel goes very slowly in peacetime. And when a war occurs, then suddenly this rotation is 10 times, 100 times as fast," he said. That leaves Camp Jomsborg with an unusual training dynamic. Ukrainians bring lessons learned from a fast-changing war, while Western partners offer conventional military expertise that some Ukrainian units never had time to build. Molde said both groups can "evolve in parallel."

item.title: American just gave its largest Boeing jets a major business class makeover. See how the cabin changed.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.06
American Airlines' largest Boeing widebody plane just got a major makeover. On Wednesday, the airline unveiled its new Flagship business class suites for its 20-strong Boeing 777-300ER fleet. American said it's the most premium-packed jet in the US, with 144 premium seats in total: 70 business-class suites, 44 premium economy seats, and 30 extra-legroom Main Cabin Extra seats. The 777-300ER is the third aircraft type American has fitted with the upgraded Flagship Suite. The cabin debuted on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s in June 2025 and later launched on the Airbus A321XLR in December 2025. Customers experienced the new Flagship interior for the first time on a flight from New York-JFK to Buenos Aires on Wednesday, and it features a lot of new perks compared to the old version. Business-class finally has doors, as well as more storage, more space, and better entertainment. Perhaps most notably, it doesn't have Flagship First, the last of its kind among US carriers. The distinctive cabin will no longer be available for booking from November 19 amid low demand and customer preference for a better business class. American — and the broader airline industry — continue to bet on premium travel as passengers remain willing to pay more for added comforts. Earlier this year, United Airlines announced a new "Elevated" interior for its Boeing 787s, featuring 99 business-class and premium-economy seats. Delta has also announced new cabins for its future Airbus A350-1000s, set to debut in 2027, with premium seats making up 50% of the jet. Business-class seats are highly profitable and account for a significant part of airlines' ticket revenue, helping pad their bottom lines even as some consumers pull back on spending and the conflict in the Middle East drives up fuel prices. In the airline's July earnings call, American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said that much of that revenue is from affluent customers, saying, "Nearly 60% of our revenue comes from households making $150,000 or more, and so that's demand that's more likely to hold up through economic uncertainty." Here's a closer look at how American is capitalizing on the premium boom, and how its new Flagship Suite compares to the old one. American's previous 777-300ER business class debuted back in 2013. The old version, pictured, had 52 seats and was a major upgrade for its time. It differed from the unpopular 2×2×2 and 2×3×2 layouts American had installed on other Boeing widebodies, which forced window-seat flyers to crawl over their neighbors to access the aisle, while some were stuck in middle seats. It also offered better seatback screens, a more comfortable and private sleeping setup, and a walk-up snack bar, stocked with drinks, fruit, chips, and cookies. The latter will remain available in American's new 777-300ER business class. The new Flagship Business maintains a 1×2×1 layout. The configuration, pictured in the bottom image, will include one seat angled in by the window and two in the middle angled toward each other, with a privacy divider between them. Every passenger will retain direct aisle access. The new seats, which span 19 rows, are made by Elevate Aircraft Seating (formerly Adient Aerospace) and are also used on American's 787s. The top photo is the old version, which had 52 seats — 18 fewer than the new Flagship. It also now features ever-popular sliding doors. Among the most highly requested perks from premium travelers are sliding doors. American's old version didn't have the door but instead had a large curved wing for privacy. The new door is also fully certified and doesn't need to be locked open, as was the case with the airline's A321XLR doors at launch. Those have since been approved by the Federal Aviation Administration. To pack in 70 business-class seats, American shaved an inch of legroom. According to the airline seating information website SeatMaps, the previous 777 business class, pictured, had one more inch of legroom, 42 inches now versus 43 before — a negligible difference. "When retrofitting any aircraft, we utilize the space available to be able to offer a variety of products for customers to choose from," an American spokesperson told Business Insider. There are now more storage and power ports. Both versions have a cubby and nooks, but American said the new version, pictured right, offers more storage space than the previous one (left), including a dedicated drink surface, shelves, and a laptop slot. Both versions offer charging via USB-A and AC ports, but the new one also includes wireless charging and USB-C. The seatback screen is also a few inches wider. All seatback screens in business class feature 17.5-inch 4K displays with Bluetooth — both significant upgrades from the previous screens. There's also a remote, but it isn't touchscreen. The seat also has a "Do Not Disturb" mode, adjustable ambient lighting, and a large tray table. There is a patented chaise lounge mode. American's unique chaise-lounge mode, which is also on the 787, allows passengers to sit upright and lean against the suite shell with their legs stretched out onto the lie-flat bed, like they're lounging on a beach chair. A patented second seatbelt keeps them secure in this position. Flagship Preferred Suites replace Flagship First. The eight Flagship First suites, complete with a swivel chair that creates a small office, are now Flagship Preferred: eight oversized suites with an ottoman that accommodates an additional passenger, allowing families to dine or socialize together, or colleagues to meet. The special nook, which takes advantage of the extra space in the bulkhead rows, is also on the 787s. Passengers can book the 777 Preferred at no additional fee, though American may monetize it in the future, as other carriers have. For example, United's similar Polaris Studio starts at $499 to add. Here's what Flagship First looked like. Flagship Business gets access to the lounge. Flagship travelers get priority check-in, boarding, security, and baggage handling, as well as access to the Flagship lounge, where available. Onboard meals are chef-curated, and the plane is stocked with premium wines and spirits. Flyers also get an amenity kit, and the linens include a cool-touch dual-sided pillow, a blanket, and a mattress pad. AAdvantage loyalty members also get access to free high-speed WiFi. The jet also includes a new premium economy cabin. The 44 upgraded premium economy seats — up from 28 — offer better privacy and space, along with elevated meals, Bluetooth connectivity, water bottle storage, wireless charging, USB-C and AC power ports, adjustable headrests, and calf and foot rests. It's considered the middle-ground in terms of price and comfort between business class and coach. Still, the 777 is so wide that American can fit eight across, meaning there are two middle seats per row. Economy was also retrofitted. American revamped the old coach and extra legroom seats with better padding, inflight entertainment, and Bluetooth connectivity. It maintains its 10-abreast seating configuration, with 216 seats in total: 186 in Main Cabin and 30 in Main Cabin Extra. Overall, the plane has 330 seats — the previous setup had 304. American's retrofitted 777-300ER will fly to five cities. American has rapidly expanded its international network to cash in on long-haul premium demand — cabins that sell for thousands of dollars to destinations across Europe, Asia, and beyond. The 777-300ER's international routes include London, Tokyo, São Paulo, Buenos Aires, and Sydney.

item.title: Walmart's copycat strategy: Restaurant delivery is its latest use of heft to break into established markets
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.05
Walmart got its start in 1962 selling general merchandise as a discount store in Rogers, Arkansas. Founder Sam Walton was constantly on the lookout for new retail concepts to try, and he wasn't shy about borrowing ideas from other successful entrepreneurs. "He just tried things, and he would learn, and if it didn't work, it wasn't a failure," CEO John Furner said during a conversation with reporters at Walmart's headquarters in June. "We just learned from it." Last week, Walmart moved to grow its delivery service in a partnership with Dunkin', putting the company on a collision course with delivery services like DoorDash and Uber Eats. The retailer will eventually offer delivery from most of the 10,000 Dunkin' locations across the US, moving onto turf long dominated by DoorDash and Uber Eats. Walmart described itself as "a rapidly emerging contender in the restaurant delivery business." That delivery experiment is a continuation of a pattern that Furner says is part of Walmart's DNA. "We constantly want to learn. We see where the world's going. Some things apply, some things don't," he said. "We'll learn from it and figure out the best way that we can accelerate the business." Here are eight bets Walmart has placed over the years in its bid to grow beyond traditional discount retailing. Home improvement One of Walmart's first attempts at branching out came in 1975 with the launch of the Sav-Co Home Improvement Center chain. The brand didn't take off, and Walmart shifted its focus to adding new features to its stores. While local hardware stores were common in this era, large-store formats were relatively uncommon. Home Depot didn't open its first stores until 1979. Pharmacy One of Walmart's early in-store experiments was in the pharmacy business, which began in 1978 and has since grown into one of the company's key business lines. Walmart dispensed an estimated $36.8 billion in prescriptions last year, making it the fifth largest pharmacy in the US, according to the Drug Channels Institute, which tracks the pharmaceutical industry. More recently, Walmart has stepped up prescription delivery speeds, with some orders filled in 30 minutes or less. Auto service Walmart opened its first auto care center in Oklahoma in 1979 and the service has expanded to nearly 2,600 locations across the US. Walmart's auto centers have also served as a testing ground for the company's expanding third-party marketplace, with customers able to order products like tires online that are shipped to a local store for scheduled installation. Warehouse club The 80's were a busy decade for Walmart and Sam Walton in terms of experimentation. "'82, '83 I think he opened four different formats in that two year period," Furner said in June. "Sam's Club came out of it and was really successful, and the others we decided not to go forward with." Walton's approach to the wholesale club was modeled on Saul Price's concepts FedMart and Price Club, the latter of which also inspired and eventually merged with Costco. Sam's Club now has more than 600 US locations with $90 billion in sales last year. Grocery The Walmart supercenter is a quintessentially American phenomenon, but Walton famously modeled the concept off the European hypermarket format, which combined general merchandise retail with groceries under a single roof. "It took probably five or six years until there was a store in Washington, Missouri, that worked," Furner said of Walton's attempts to adapt the hypermarket concept to the US. It still took Walmart opening about a dozen more supercenters for the idea to really gain traction, he added. There are now more than 3,500 supercenters and more than 650 neighborhood market grocery stores in the US. Walmart is the largest grocery chain in the country, pulling in roughly one in five dollars spent in the category, according to consumer analytics firm Numerator. Specialty retail About a decade ago, Walmart embarked on a flurry of merger activity, snapping up specialty retailers Bonobos, Moosejaw, and Modcloth in a bid to expand the company's reach with specialty brands and e-commerce customers. All three chains remained independent of Walmart's core operations and were subsequently sold off to other owners as the company refocused on its own offerings. Advertising In 2019, Walmart brought its advertising business in-house with what would become Walmart Connect, which sells ad space for the company's physical and digital properties. Combined with a growing third-party e-commerce marketplace and the acquisition of TV-maker Vizio, Walmart's ads business has delivered significant revenue growth in recent years. Restaurant delivery Walmart's latest bet puts the company on a course to compete more directly with food delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats. After letting grocery-delivery customers add meals from in-store Subway shops, Walmart said in September it would bring thousands of off-site Dunkin' locations to the service. Walmart has already established itself as a powerhouse in fast delivery for merchandise, groceries, and medicine — now it's set to fulfill more of what other chains sell too.

item.title: Climb aboard YP 700, a US Naval Academy training vessel where midshipmen take a maritime version of driver's ed
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.04
At the United States Naval Academy, every midshipman learns to drive. Their driver's ed curriculum doesn't involve slow circles in empty parking lots or parallel parking tests. Instead, the future naval leaders learn how to drive, steer, and navigate a ship by going out on the water and doing just that. After midshipmen learn the basics of navigation, boat handling, man-overboard maneuvers, and standard commands in the classroom, they put their knowledge into practice on training vessels known as yard patrol craft. During my visit to the Naval Academy in August, I got to climb aboard the yard patrol craft YP 700 to see how midshipmen learn shiphandling and navigation on the job. Take a look. Midshipmen at the US Naval Academy practice their seamanship skills on yard patrol boats. Training is held both in the classroom and aboard yard patrol craft during the school year. In the summertime, midshipmen embark on longer trips where they manage every aspect of the journey, from navigation to cooking. While underway, midshipmen are supervised by experienced craftmasters, who are responsible for the safe operation of the vessels but largely take a hands-off approach to the training. I got an exclusive look inside one of these training vessels. YP 700 measures 108 feet long and can hold around 30 people. With two diesel engines, it can reach a maximum speed of about 12 knots (about 14 mph). It has a range of 1,800 nautical miles and can remain underway for up to five days without refueling. In July, midshipmen sailed four yard patrol craft to Baltimore and New York City as part of the International Naval Review for America's 250th anniversary. Aside from special events such as Fleet Weeks, yard patrol craft aren't usually open for public tours. My tour started at the bow, where the wildcat, a toothed wheel that grips and moves the anchor chain, helps raise and lower the anchor. The wildcat is the one piece of machinery that midshipmen don't operate themselves since doing so incorrectly can, as one craftmaster told me, result in losing a finger. However, midshipmen do practice other aspects of anchoring, such as positioning the boat correctly. The pilothouse functions as the control center of the ship, housing the main helm, or steering wheel, and navigational equipment. The main helm controls the ship's rudder. Midshipmen also learn to steer the ship using just its port and starboard engines, which are controlled by separate levers. Midshipmen learn how to maneuver the vessel using the engines if normal rudder steering is lost. The navigation table houses the Voyage Management System, or VMS, which midshipmen learn how to use during their youngster, or sophomore, year. The table itself is a holdover from an era when paper charts were central to maritime navigation. Midshipmen today train extensively on electronic navigation systems, though they also learn traditional chart plotting. The VMS shows a live feed of other vessels in the area using data from the Automatic Identification System, or AIS. Through AIS, vessels broadcast their name, call sign, speed, course, and other key information that can help other ships contact and navigate around them. AIS complements radar by providing identification information on vessels transmitting a signal. The VMS displays that data, as well as useful chart information, including shallow or shoal water that could pose a grounding risk. The boat's sound tube is a relic from the days before handheld radios, but it still serves an amusing purpose as midshipmen learn the ropes. The craftmaster serving as my tour guide said he offers the sound tube to midshipmen as a place where they can scream out their frustration and relieve some stress before returning to their duties. He said it works very well. Below deck, the ship's craftmaster and other crew sleep in dedicated berths during trips. Midshipmen stay in bunks, known as racks, on another level further below deck, with six to 12 people to a room. Midshipmen are in charge of planning and preparing meals in the ship's galley. A midshipman designated as the supply officer creates the meal plan and assigns cooking duties. The galley features all of the basics, including a stove, oven, toaster, and microwave. Sometimes, crews will also bring an air fryer or a grill. Meals are eaten in seating booths near the galley or out on the deck in cooperative weather. The galley is the coldest space on the ship in the summertime, so midshipmen often eat their meals downstairs. A multipurpose common space occasionally serves as a classroom, briefing room, and lounge, but most of the instruction happens on the job. When the boat is underway, midshipmen learn to expect the unexpected. Craftmasters will throw a life ring overboard and see how long it takes them to notice, or suddenly declare "Man overboard!" to test their reaction time and knowledge of the correct procedures. The classroom space on board, it turns out, is barely used at all.

item.title: Emirates is bringing one of business travelers' favorite features to its premium economy cabins
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.04
For years, privacy on planes was reserved for the wealthiest travelers. Now that's changing. Emirates unveiled a new premium-economy seat on Thursday, with a unique privacy screen. As well as being more private, the new seat is easier to recline and raise the legrest with electric controls. Plus, it reclines in a cradle position, which avoids intruding on the passenger behind. While Japan Airlines was the first to introduce electric controls in premium economy, Emirates' new seat also uses them to control the privacy divider, which extends to the full height of the seat. Wealthy travelers have grown more accustomed to privacy since Emirates first introduced a sliding door to its first-class suites in 2003. In the years since, they've become essentially de rigueur in business class. However, premium economy passengers have typically had little to separate them from their neighbors. Many premium-economy cabins lack any privacy screens, instead using a small panel that extends from the headrest. United Airlines introduced a divider in its Premium Plus cabin last year, although it does not extend to the seat's full height. While electric controls can make life easier for passengers, they are at a higher risk of malfunctioning than manual controls, increasing maintenance costs. Emirates' new seat also includes the U-Dream headrest that it revealed for the economy cabin at July's Farnborough Airshow. It features two side wings that fold down and inward. "The U-Dream changes the game if the person wants to sleep — by supporting the neck in full," Emirates President Tim Clark said in the press release. "No more neck pillows needed." Business Insider tried the new headrest at Farnborough and found it to be a genuine game changer. Emirates' new premium-economy seats also feature wireless charging, and a tray table with an integrated phone holder — if you need a second screen in addition to the 13.3-inch 4K one on the seatback. Emirates did not say when the new seat will debut, other than it being "on board soon," nor which routes would see it first. It will be available on newly delivered Airbus A350 airplanes. They have 28 premium-economy seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. The seats are 20 inches wide and have a pitch of 39 inches — the distance between the same spot on one seat and that of the row behind. Emirates was relatively late to the premium-economy trend, first adding the cabin to its flagship Airbus A380 aircraft in early 2021. The cabin has become especially popular since the pandemic. With travelers willing to spend extra money for more luxury, premium economy bridges the gap to business class.

item.title: A veteran chief engineer building a flying taxi shared the one piece of advice he'd give his 25-year-old self
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.85
David King is the chief engineer at Vertical Aerospace, a British company developing an eVTOL — an electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft — intended to work like a flying taxi. If he could give his 25-year-old self one piece of advice, King said, it would be: "Don't be afraid of the unknown." "Just discover, and embrace the discovery, and learn as you go, but get to discovery safely and effectively," he told Business Insider. King, who has more than 35 years of experience in aerospace, spoke to Business Insider at July's Farnborough Airshow, where Vertical's VX4 prototype became the first eVTOL to publicly perform a transition flight. Its wing-mounted propellers tilted so it could fly like an airplane, before transitioning back to land like a helicopter. King began his career after earning a graduate degree from MIT in 1989. He later became the chief engineer on programs at Bell and Leonardo before joining Vertical in 2023. Looking back, he said he had come to appreciate "how much of a rewarding experience it is to learn something new every day." That's a handy perspective for a company building a new type of aircraft. eVTOLs are designed to function like helicopters but make much less noise, so the hope is they could be used over cities more frequently. The goal is to transform commutes and other short trips. For example, Vertical says its Valo air taxi could fly the 22 miles from Miami Airport to Fort Lauderdale in 11 minutes, compared to an hour by car. Most manufacturers have said they expect a seat on board to cost about the same as a luxury rideshare option like an Uber Black. However, there is still work to be done for air taxis to be certified by aviation regulators. "When you test it at the next higher level of integration, you're going to have some level of discovery," King said. "Get there quickly, then you learn, adjust your models, and then go test it." For King, the key is making those discoveries without taking unnecessary risks. He said young engineers should put "guardrails" around testing so that they can learn safely, but move quickly enough to avoid becoming stuck trying to make a model perfect before testing it. He recalled getting discouraged by unexpected results when he was younger, but embracing this has been a huge help. "Once people get energized by discovery as opposed to discouraged by discovery, you can see the iterations happen quickly," he said. Vertical is targeting entry into commercial service in 2029.

item.title: OpenAI's ad for its latest model looks straight out of the movie 'WALL-E' — and people have thoughts
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.59
At this point, there's hardly any reason to get off the couch. OpenAI released a demonstration video for its new Astra model on Thursday. In the clip, people sit or pace before a large screen, barking orders at the model, which heeds their demands — including requests to list furniture on eBay and order takeout — almost instantly. The futuristic video, which so far has more than 75 million views on X, sparked a spirited online debate: How much is too much automation? And how long until humanity starts to resemble the sedentary space people from "WALL-E?" "Give humans nothing to do, nothing to build, nothing to struggle for long enough, and Idiocracy stops looking like satire and starts looking like a roadmap," one user wrote on X.
