OpenAI's new model The ChatGPT maker called Astra "the world's most intelligent and aligned model" in a press release on Thursday. OpenAI said it applied lessons from what it called the "Hugging Face incident," in which rogue agents hacked into the platform's servers during a test, to make Astra safer. By Friday, some users on X were proudly displaying highly detailed 3D scenes created on Blender via prompts on Astra. GPT-6 Astra vs Fable 5.1 in Blender… The gap in visual quality is actually crazy 👀 AI is getting dangerously good at turning prompts into fully built 3D scenes. Which one would you pick? pic.twitter.com/SIFmpzlEzu Other users posted clips from video games they designed using the new model. Users said the games were easy to create and highly steerable. Astra (GPT-6) is here!!! I've had early access and tested it like crazy with things like games, code, writing, browser control, presentations and general knowledge work. This is the best model I've ever used. Period. (Incredible demos below in this thread ⬇️) Here's my take… pic.twitter.com/t1CMMSBelQ A dystopian future Astra quickly drew comparisons to various movies in which characters rely on AI to the point of being unable to live without it. Some comparisons were flattering — like Jarvis, Iron Man's digital companion who controls his armor and occasionally delivers dry jokes. Other people, though, said that with models like Astra, it was only a matter of time before humanity regressed into a slothful, inert species with no reason to move, travel, or work. Thanks. Even more lazy people now. Its going to be like the people from WALL-E soon pic.twitter.com/KVsDVJB5UH In "WALL-E," the 2008 Pixar classic, humanity abandoned Earth after it became filled with garbage. They left the planet aboard a giant spaceship, and 700 years later, the population evolved into obese screen-watchers who got their nutrition through straws. "You know, survival, longevity, health, food, regenerative food, all that stuff," the film's director, Andrew Stanton, told NPR in 2008 when it first came out. "So what's the point of living? And so it was like this hellacious, perpetual vacation." Users on X also compared the technology to the 2013 film "Her," directed by Spike Jonze, in which the main character, played by Joaquin Phoenix, falls in love with an AI companion before discovering that it's also in love with more than 600 other people.

After the conflict started, prices rose sharply across the US. AAA data show the national average peaked in May at roughly $4.56 per gallon, then zigzagged through the end of August, averaging $4.09. Now, as average prices continue to creep up, hitting $4.15 on Friday, AAA expects this to be the most expensive Labor Day on record for gas. We also looked at the gas prices on September 4 and compared them with prices reported one year ago. "The national average has never been above $4 per gallon on Labor Day. item.title: Nvidia has built a $99 billion equity portfolio from almost scratch in 2 years
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.38
Nvidia has built a nearly $100 billion equity portfolio from virtually scratch in just two years by investing in other tech companies. The AI chipmaker, led by CEO Jensen Huang, held $99 billion in equity investments as of July 26, according to its latest earnings report. That included roughly $48 billion in publicly traded stocks and other marketable securities, $48 billion in shares of private companies and other non-marketable securities, and $3 billion in equity-method investments. Its equity portfolio surged 14-fold in a year from about $7 billion last summer, and 45-fold from $2.2 billion two summers ago. The company also reported a further $25 billion in equity investment commitments as of July 26. Nvidia's quarterly portfolio disclosure offered a glimpse at its public US stock portfolio as of June 30. It held a $30 billion stake in Intel, a $21 billion position in SpaceX, and investments in CoreWeave, Coherent, Synopsys, and Nokia, each worth between $2 billion and $5 billion. The huge increase in Nvidia's equity holdings has vaulted it into the ranks of the biggest tech investors. It still trails the likes of Alphabet, which had a $232 billion equity portfolio at the end of June, including $94 billion of SpaceX shares following its IPO in June. Nvidia stock has rocketed from below $15 at the start of 2023 to $228 at Thursday's close. That 15-fold increase in under three years has catapulted its market capitalization to $5.5 trillion, making it the world's most valuable company. The chipmaker has become the premier enabler of the AI boom by providing the types of semiconductors needed to power the nascent technology, financing the AI infrastructure buildout, and investing in its AI peers. A Nvidia spokesperson pointed Business Insider to finance chief Colette Kress, saying on the company's latest earnings call that frontier AI labs' ability to improve their products, attract more users, and generate more revenue was being "limited by compute," so Nvidia was "needed to help power this flywheel" and had thus invested almost $50 billion in them. In its latest earnings report, Nvidia said that it makes equity investments to "enhance our growth opportunities, cultivate our ecosystem, and strengthen our competitive position." However, Michael Burry of "The Big Short" fame has said Nvidia is "overreaching" in its efforts to juice its growth by financing and investing in customers of its chips. Similarly, former "Shark Tank" investor Mark Cuban has said it's "truly scary" how reliant the AI boom is on Nvidia "funding everyone and anyone."

item.title: Tesla's Cybercab launch catches the eye of US auto safety regulator
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.33
Tesla's Cybercab is live in Austin. Now, regulators in Washington are asking to check the EV-maker's homework. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, or NHTSA, opened an audit inquiry late Thursday into Tesla's Cybercab certification. The move came hours after Tesla's commercial deployment of a small number of Cybercabs in Austin, which joined its robotaxi network. Texas DMV records list 45 Cybercabs registered to Tesla. The vehicle has yet to be made available to purchase to consumers. "NHTSA fully supports the safe development and deployment of automated vehicles," Jonathan Morrison, the agency's administrator, wrote in a statement sent to Business Insider. "But as the federal regulator, we need to ensure that all of our laws are followed." NHTSA's announcement doesn't order Tesla to halt Cybercab deployments — the agency hasn't made any comment on the vehicle's safety or compliance. Instead, NHTSA will examine Tesla's technical data and the processes behind the automaker's self-certification. Automakers typically certify their own vehicles' compliance with federal rules. Tesla told NHTSA that the Cybercab complies with applicable federal safety standards. The certification could pose thorny questions for Tesla, given today's vehicle rules. The Cybercab doesn't have conventional human controls — such as a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors — that are required by current federal safety standards. NHTSA will examine whether Tesla was correct in determining that some of those requirements do not apply to its automated vehicle. Tesla is not the first company to confront the full-autonomy regulatory challenge. In July, NHTSA gave Amazon-owned Zoox a temporary exemption to deploy its own steering-wheel-free robotaxis commercially. Tesla is taking a different route: It certified that the Cybercab meets all applicable federal rules, even as NHTSA is still working to update standards, including one governing brake pedals, for driverless vehicles. Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

item.title: Taylor Swift's $100 million real estate portfolio includes houses in Nashville, Rhode Island, and Beverly Hills
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.17
Taylor Swift will never be out of style — or at least out of homes. The superstar has built a real estate portfolio worth at least $100 million, according to property records reviewed by Business Insider. She's used trusts and limited liability companies (LLCs) to buy homes throughout the US. Swift reached billionaire status in 2023, and her record-breaking Eras Tour is a big factor in her fortune. Swift's net worth has continued to grow with the 2025 release of her album and film, "The Life of a Showgirl;" she also wrote and performed an original song for the "Toy Story 5" soundtrack in June 2026. This year, Swift also married Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce in a star-studded wedding. Kelce brings several multimillion-dollar properties into the marriage, including homes in Kansas and Missouri. He also recently bought a sprawling lakefront mansion in Ohio for $5.35 million. Take a look at some of the homes where Taylor Swift may be settling into married life. Jordan Hart and Britney Nguyen contributed to a previous version of this story. Swift made her first major purchase in 2009 at age 19, buying a 4,000-square-foot, three-bedroom penthouse in The Adelicia in Nashville, Tennessee, for $1.99 million. Not only is The Adelicia close to Nashville's Music Row, but it also has a private garage, heated pool, and fitness center, according to the building's website. After purchasing her penthouse, Architectural Digest reported that Swift also bought a one-bedroom unit directly below it that year for an undisclosed amount. As of 2021, the appraised value of the apartment is over $3.7 million, according to public property records viewed by Business Insider. Swift told Vulture that she designed the penthouse herself. When she spoke to the publication in 2013, she had a photo on display of Kanye West interrupting her at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards. Under the photo she reportedly wrote, "Life is full of little interruptions." Swift reportedly bought the Northumberland Estate in Forest Hills, Tennessee, in 2011 for $2.5 million. The estate sits on 5 acres and has an appraised property value of about $3.7 million as of 2021. Although multiple outlets — including The Wall Street Journal — have reported that Swift owns the mansion, Business Insider was unable to confirm her ownership via property records in 2024. We've reached out to her representatives in an attempt to clarify if she still owns the property. The Northumberland Estate is a Greek Revival-style home that was built around 1934. It formerly belonged to Guilford Dudley Jr., who served as the US ambassador to Denmark, WSJ reported. Swift bought an 11,000-square-foot colonial-style mansion in Watch Hill, Rhode Island, for $17.75 million in 2013. The home, formerly known as Holiday House, was built in 1904 and previously owned by composer Rebekah Harkness, the wife of William Hale "Bill" Harkness, an heir of the Standard Oil fortune. Swift wrote the "Folklore" album track "The Last Great American Dynasty" about Rebekah, who was a prominent socialite. Swift reportedly paid for the home in cash. The mansion has eight bedrooms, eight fireplaces, and a pool. "I got the house when I was in my early twenties as a place for my family to congregate and be together," Swift told Entertainment Weekly, saying that she learned about Harkness "as soon as I was being walked through [her former Rhode Island] home." Swift is known for throwing Fourth of July parties at the house, which sits at the highest point in Watch Hill and offers views of Little Narragansett Bay. In 2024, several photos of her with her famous friends and now-husband were snapped at the home. Zillow now estimates the property's value at nearly $35 million. Swift bought the Beverly Hills mansion known as the Goldwyn Estate in 2015 for $25 million. Zillow now estimates the property's value at nearly $35 million. Swift reportedly bought the estate from the Goldwyn family through an LLC. It belonged to the legendary Hollywood producer who was part of the iconic Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer film studio, and reportedly hosted old Hollywood stars such as Clark Gable and Bette Davis. The mansion has six bedrooms, a tennis court, a whole apartment for guests, and a swimming pool. In 2017, the home was granted historic landmark status, WSJ reported. Swift welcomed herself to New York by buying two penthouse units in Tribeca's Sugar Loaf building in 2014 for $19.95 million. She had the penthouses converted into an 8,309-square-foot duplex, which now has 10 bedrooms and 10 bathrooms. Swift bought the penthouses from "The Lord of the Rings" director Peter Jackson through an LLC. Three years later, in 2017, she bought the townhouse next door for $18 million, and in 2018, she purchased yet another apartment in the Sugar Loaf building for $9.75 million. All four of her reported NYC apartments can be linked by LLCs that share the same tax addresses on property records. Andrew Azoulay, a real-estate agent in Manhattan, told The Wall Street Journal that he advised Swift to buy the townhouse to act as a private garage and to buy the second-floor apartment to connect the garage to her duplex in the Sugar Loaf building. Swift's townhouse has been the target of break-in attempts over the years. In 2023, a man was arrested for trying to gain access to the building while Swift was attending the Kansas City Chiefs game versus the Bills in Buffalo. She still owns the property.

item.title: Meet the 52 women competing to be the next Miss America
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.50
It's almost time to crown the next Miss America. On September 6, 52 women from around the country will gather at the Palm Beach County Convention Center in West Palm Beach, Florida, for the chance to win the coveted title. The winner will be crowned by Miss America 2026 Cassie Donnegan and will take home a $50,000 scholarship. Before you watch the competition — which will stream on PageantVision.com at 7 p.m. ET — meet the 52 women competing for the crown. Alabama: Ruby Tilghman Ruby Tilghman, 22, graduated from the University of Alabama with a degree in chemistry. She is an incoming student at the university's Heersink School of Medicine. Tilghman previously represented Florida at the Miss America's Teen competition in 2021. Tilghman is an avid hiker who has visited 28 national parks. She is also a recipient of the President's Volunteer Service Lifetime Achievement Award. Alaska: Nora Andrews Nora Andrews, 20, is a senior at Grand Canyon University, where she is studying psychology and professional writing. She is hoping to earn a Ph.D. in clinical psychology and a certification in sex and relational education and therapy. Andrews is also an advocate for suicide prevention and mental health awareness. Arizona: Victoria Vredevoogd Victoria Vredevoogd, 25, is a law student at the Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law at Arizona State University. The pageant queen founded and serves as president of The Gender Violence Project, an organization at ASU that advocates for survivors and provides free legal resources. She also wrote and published her own fantasy novel, titled "A Legend of Golden Shadows." Arkansas: Ava Weeks Ava Weeks, 20, is a student at Ouachita Baptist University. She hopes to become a secondary English teacher. Weeks became an advocate for passenger safety after witnessing a terrible car accident when she was a teenager, according to her Miss America bio. Her community initiative is "Every Seat. Every Ride. Buckle Up." Weeks has won over $50,000 in scholarships from competing in the Miss America system. California: Sharlize True Trujillo Sharlize True Trujillo, 22, is pursuing a degree in gender studies and a minor in film and television from the University of California, Los Angeles. She is planning to attend law school and study entertainment law. The pageant queen is also a dancer, actress, and content creator. She has more than 2 million followers on TikTok. Colorado: Gabrielle Burns Gabrielle Burns, 23, is pursuing a master's degree from the University of Colorado Boulder. She is studying to become a speech-language pathologist. Burns is an advocate for communication disorders and disabilities. She's also a professional ballroom dancer. Connecticut: Christa Steiner Christa Steiner, 27, graduated from the Manhattan School of Music, where she earned a degree in vocal performance and musical theater. Steiner is a professional singer and voice teacher. She is using her Miss America platform to advocate for increased access to mental health treatment. Delaware: Anaya Harrison Anaya Harrison, 24, earned both her undergraduate and graduate degrees from the Biden School of Public Policy at the University of Delaware. She plans to attend law school. Harrison works as a congressional aide in the US House of Representatives, where she "helps constituents navigate federal agencies," according to her Miss America bio. District of Columbia: Evelyn Smith Evelyn Smith, 25, graduated from Oklahoma City University with a bachelor's degree in philosophy and minors in political science and studio art. She was the first Black woman to win Miss Oklahoma's Teen, and she made it to the top nine at the Miss America's Teen 2018 competition. Smith has certified more than 1,000 individuals in CPR. She used her own skills to save her mother's life during a heart attack, according to her Miss America bio. Florida: Alexandra de Roos Alexandra de Roos, 23, is an honors student at the University of South Florida, where she is studying psychology. She plans to attend medical school and become a neuropsychiatrist. The pageant queen was previously a student at the School of American Ballet, but her dancing career was cut short after a traumatic brain injury. She founded The Blue Project nonprofit to advocate for brain injury education and healing through the arts, according to her Miss Florida bio. Georgia: Sophia Wootten Sophia Wootten, 21, is pursuing a degree in communication sciences and disorders at the University of Georgia. She is planning to become a pediatric audiologist. Wootten made history as the first Miss America contestant with a cleft lip and palate. She has undergone 20 reconstructive surgeries and wears hearing aids. The pageant queen wants to use her platform to "redefine what representation looks like for children with disabilities," according to her Miss America bio. Hawaii: Carly Yoshida Carly Yoshida, 26, earned a degree in social sciences from the University of Hawai'i - West O'ahu and plans to pursue a professional meteorology degree. Yoshida is a field reporter, digital content producer, and on-air weather personality for KITV 4 Island News, an ABC affiliate in Honolulu. She previously won Miss Hawaii's Teen in 2016. Idaho: Déja Fitzwater Déja Fitzwater, 21, is studying communications at the University of Idaho. She is an avid 4-H volunteer and won Miss Oregon's Teen in 2022. Fitzwater, an advocate for agricultural literacy, is using her platform to "help young people better understand the people, science, and industries behind their food and natural resources," according to her Miss America bio. Illinois: Kate Dimmett Kate Dimmett, 23, graduated from both the Kelley School of Business and the Jacobs School of Music at Indiana University. The pageant queen is a professional violinist. Dimmett is the president of Notable Measures, a nonprofit she launched at 13 to expand access to music education. According to her Miss America bio, she has raised over $90,000 and provided 170 grants through her organization. She previously won Miss Indiana's Teen in 2021. Indiana: Ellise Edwards Ellise Edwards, 22, graduated from the University of South Florida. She is a content creator with over 127,000 followers on TikTok, where she shares videos of her curly-hair routine and her experience as a postgrad. Edwards wants to help businesses grow their online presence "through strategic social media marketing," according to her Miss America bio. Iowa: McKenzie Kerry McKenzie Kerry, 27, graduated from the Belk College of Business at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. She has been involved in organizations including Iowa Jobs for America's Graduates and Big Brothers Big Sisters Workplace Mentoring. Kerry was recruited into Principal Financial Group's three-year leadership development program. She currently serves as a learning and development consultant. Kansas: Sophie Lewis Sophie Lewis, 23, graduated with honors from the University of Kansas with a degree in biochemistry and a minor in business. Lewis works as a medical sales consultant and is helping expand access to biomarker blood testing for early lung cancer detection, according to her Miss America bio. The pageant queen made history as the first Asian American woman to win the title of Miss Kansas. Kentucky: Reagan Earlywine Reagan Earlywine, 24, is a third-year dental student at the University of Louisville. She is a recipient of the Excellence in Dental Gross and Neurological Anatomy award. Earlywine plans to become an orthodontist someday. She is using her platform to advocate for access to preventive oral healthcare. Louisiana: Shelby Bordelon Shelby Bordelon, 24, is pursuing her master's in strategic communication at Southeastern Louisiana University. She founded Claire's Promise, Inc., a nonprofit organization that works to prevent impaired driving, after her friend was killed by an impaired driver. She is also a spokesperson for MADD Louisiana. Maine: Ruthie Gusler Ruthie Gusler, 19, is studying business administration at the University of Maine at Farmington, where she plays soccer. She hopes to become a real estate agent. Gusler created the Wonder Kids community service initiative to advocate for children who survive abuse. Maryland: Gianna Romero Gianna Romero, 21, is a student at Stevenson University, where she studies business communication. She wants to work in sports marketing after college, interning in the athletics department at Calvert Hall College High School. Romero advocates for healthy relationships, sharing her own experience of being in an abusive relationship for two years to help others. Massachusetts: Ashlyn Mercier Ashlyn Mercier, 25, is a police officer. She earned her undergraduate degree in national security from the University of New Haven in Connecticut and her master's degree in criminal justice from Boston University. Mercier created Nick's Courage: One Smile Goes a Mile, an initiative designed to support children with cancer. Her brother had cancer twice as a child, so the program is close to her heart. Michigan: Grace Hanke Grace Hanke, 19, is studying mechanical engineering at the University of Detroit Mercy, participating in the school's accelerated master's program. She wants to ensure other young women have access to STEM opportunities, so she created the Engineer Her Future US initiative. Hanke has also partnered with several organizations to promote STEM education and access nationally. Minnesota: Anna Brennan Anna Brennan, 20, hopes to become a news anchor, so she is studying journalism at the University of St. Thomas. She is also a professional ballerina. Brennan created MediaWELL, an initiative that aims to provide media literacy education to people of all ages. Mississippi: Jane Granberry Jane Granberry, 23, is a student in the MBA program at the University of Mississippi. She used her integrated marketing and communications degree from the school as an influencer marketing and PR coordinator at Tarte Cosmetics. She launched Literacy Without Limits, which provides literacy education and tools to people in Mississippi. She was first runner-up in the Miss Mississippi pageant in 2024 and 2025 before being crowned queen. Missouri: Tabitha Crain Tabitha Crain, 24, is a law student at the University of Missouri. She wants to use her degree to advocate for survivors of domestic violence. According to her Miss America bio, she has raised over $500,000 to support survivors of domestic and sexual abuse. Crain is passionate about fitness, as she is a former cheerleader and gymnast. She teaches spin classes in her free time. Montana: Adella Harris Adella Harris, 19, studies political science at Montana State University, where she is an honors student. She wants to go to law school after college and hopes to run for office someday. Harris created the Made for More initiative, encouraging children to chase their dreams. Nebraska: Lexi Nolda Lexi Nolda, 22, earned a bachelor's degree in nutrition and health sciences from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. After skin cancer affected members of her family, Nolda hopes to someday become a dermatology nurse practitioner. Nolda advocates for skin cancer prevention, and she hopes to expand that work if she is crowned Miss America. Nevada: Mariah Larronde Mariah Larronde, 27, got her bachelor's degree in digital audiences and media analysis at Arizona State University. She plans to pursue a master's in data science while working toward her goal of becoming an actress. Larronde wants to support children who lose a parent or have a parent struggling with an illness, so she created the Hidden Caregiver Network. New Hampshire: Lauren Plank Lauren Plank, 21, is a student in an accelerated master's program at the University of New Hampshire. Her goal is to become an elementary school teacher. She believes in the power of volunteering, so she created a program to encourage children to get involved with service work. New Jersey: Kylie Gene Wright Kylie Gene Wright, 23, is studying business administration. She also works at AmeriKick Karate Studio, where she uses her second-degree black belt to teach classes. Wright is an advocate for survivors of domestic and sexual abuse, and she serves as the East Coast Chapter President of T.A.K.E. Defense, a role in which she has raised over $10,000, according to her Miss America bio. New Mexico: Katarina Blakeslee Katarina Blakeslee, 26, got her bachelor's degrees in public health and theater performance from Tulane University and holds an MFA in screenwriting from the University of Southern California. She has worked on films and TV shows for studios like A24 and Netflix. Blakeslee is pursuing a Master of Anesthesia program at the University of New Mexico and works in her state's only Level One Trauma Center. She is also passionate about literacy advocacy and wrote the children's book "Valiant and the Bubble." New York: Madison Oh Madison Oh, 21, studies English, dance, and business management at Columbia University. She would love to dance on Broadway someday. She advocates for the Minds Matter: Education Empowers initiative, which supports students applying to college and seeking career opportunities. North Carolina: Lauryn Mallard Lauryn Mallard, 26, has a bachelor's degree in nutritional science from the University of North Carolina at Greensboro and an MBA in healthcare management from High Point University. She wants to become a physician assistant. Mallard has worked with the Make-A-Wish Foundation for almost 20 years, raising money for pediatric cancer care and research. North Dakota: Emma Tong Emma Tong, 23, studied biology at the University of Alabama and will attend the University of North Dakota School of Medicine and Health Sciences to become a doctor. She wants to be a radiation oncologist. She was previously named Miss North Dakota's Outstanding Teen 2021. Ohio: Lexie Miller Lexie Miller, 23, is a cardiovascular ICU nurse who graduated from the University of Akron. Her career was inspired by her parents, who work as a first responder and a healthcare professional. Miller hopes to raise awareness for cardiovascular health. Oklahoma: Jaselyn Rossman Jaselyn Rossman, 22, has a bachelor's degree in accounting with a minor in finance from Oklahoma State University — but she's not stopping there. She plans to pursue a master's degree in the field. She's also passionate about creating work opportunities for people with disabilities and has worked with Special Olympics and The Bridges organization. In her free time, she volunteers as a presenter for Oklahoma Cares for Children and the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drug Control. Oregon: Allyssa Defillipo Allyssa Defillipo, 26, has dreams of becoming a holistic nutritionist. She works as both a manager of a chiropractic and wellness business and as a women's nutrition and fitness coach. She was inspired by her childhood in a low-income home to expand nutrition education and access to healthy foods. Defillipo has also written a children's book. Pennsylvania: Stephanie Skinner Stephanie Skinner, 21, is an advocate for children who have nontraditional upbringings. She herself was raised by a single mother who served as a US Army Major. Some of Skinner's recent accomplishments include graduating from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and performing at the FIFA World Cup Fourth of July ceremony. Puerto Rico: Annika Schneider Annika Schneider, 21, is a dancer, cheerleader, and graduate of Pfeiffer University. She has a bachelor's degree in business management and leadership. She was the first Hispanic woman to be crowned Miss North Carolina Teen, and now, as Miss Puerto Rico, she aims to advocate for the benefits of reading. Rhode Island: Mia Daley Mia Daley, 19, is an arts student at Salve Regina University. She dreams of performing on Broadway and is passionate about storytelling onstage. She's also an advocate for improving mental health through dance. She believes it has the power to heal and serve as a tool for self-expression. South Carolina: Lindsay Jones Lindsay Jones, 26, works as a national sales manager for a world-renowned tool company, where she leads a multimillion-dollar territory, according to her Miss America bio. She has an MBA and is now pursuing a Ph.D. in business. In her free time, Jones works with Big Brothers Big Sisters of America and serves on its board. South Dakota: Kianna Healy Kianna Healy, 23, is a performer. She first took the stage at age 7 and has since participated in vocal and theater productions across the country. She graduated from Pace University with degrees in film and arts and entertainment management. Healy is also passionate about animal welfare. Tennessee: Makalyn Heaslett Makalyn Heaslett, 27, has brought business to the sports world. She graduated from Auburn University, previously worked for the Chicago Cubs and Chicago White Sox, and is now an account executive for the Tennessee Titans. Heaslett is also pursuing a master's degree in sport administration at Belmont University. As a volunteer, she works with Girls Inc. to provide mentorship and leadership to young girls. She's helped raise more than $23,000 for its various organizations, according to her Miss America bio. Texas: Regan Hutsell Regan Hutsell, 25, is a former Radio City Rockette and ballerina who now aims to become a physical therapist for dancers. She's working toward her bachelor's degree in health sciences and is an advocate for self-confidence and mental health. Utah: Erika Dalton Erika Dalton, 26, is the first Japanese American to be crowned Miss Utah. She's also a Juilliard scholarship recipient, a professional violinist who's performed at Carnegie Hall, and a University of Michigan graduate with degrees in violin performance and business. Dalton also serves as a state-certified crisis advocate and volunteer for the Sexual Assault Hotline. Vermont: Hannah Roque Hannah Roque, 26, has a deep history with Miss America. Her mom was Miss Vermont 1996. Roque works in higher education and has a bachelor's degree in English and secondary education. She's also an advocate for the American Heart Association's Go Red for Women movement. Virginia: Maddie Marchant Maddie Marchant, 22, is a media and communication student at East Tennessee State University. She plans to become a journalist. She's also the founder of the Buddy Bunch Club, which provides people with disabilities the chance to learn social, academic, and professional skills. Washington: Natalie Worthy Natalie Worthy, 23, graduated from the University of Puget Sound with a music degree and is now working toward a master's degree in arts policy and administration at Ohio State University. She founded Amplify the Arts, a nonprofit organization, to merge her passions for vocal instruction and performing with her commitment to helping others. West Virginia: Elizabeth Romanek Elizabeth Romanek, 24, was a competitive dancer and D1 athlete, so she's passionate about exercise and movement. She is an ambassador of the West Virginia Physical Activity Plan. Romanek is also a master's student at Bethany College and the assistant director of admission and recruitment events at the school. Wisconsin: Jordenne Butler Jordenne Butler, 27, was inspired by her father's experience with stage four throat and neck cancer to write "Bentley Bounces Back," a children's book. She's also an advocate for resilience education and support of kids who have experienced adverse childhood experiences. Butler has a bachelor's degree in marketing and a minor in creative media from Viterbo University. Wyoming: Alyssa Medina Alyssa Medina, 22, is a sixth-grade teacher who earned her degrees in elementary and special education from the University of Wyoming. She has a sister, Briana, who's inspired Medina to support and bring joy to children who have disabilities.

item.title: Are data centers really bad for the planet?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.81
Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems. In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parcel reserved for agriculture and groundwater protection — a local green space known for its rapeseed blossoms — was rezoned in 2024 to make way for a five-building data center campus. The damage often extends beyond the site itself. Gas pipelines and power plants built to supply these facilities require their own land, fragmenting habitats and eroding soil along their routes. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Macron visits Bayeux Tapestry with King Charles, PM Andy Burnham
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.57
French President Emmanuel Macron began a two-day trip to the UK by visiting another famous new arrival from France, the Bayeux Tapestry, with King Charles III and Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel joined King Charles and Queen Camilla to walk the length of the 70-meter tapestry in the British Museum. Charles hailed the "unprecedented loan" as a "precious symbol of trust" between the UK and France, while Macron said the two countries were "as close as the threads" in the artwork. Why is the Bayeux Tapestry in London? The tapestry, which depicts the momentous events of 1066 culminating in William the Conqueror of Normandy claiming the English throne, is on temporary loan from its usual home in France. It's the first time it's touched British soil since its creation in the 11th century. The embroidery is on loan for a 10-month exhibiton opening to the public next week, on September 10. The exchange was first announced during Macron's state visit last year. Though it's thought to have been made in the British Isles, it had been on French soil ever since the 11th century. It's usually on show in Bayeux in Normandy in northern France, hence the name. The effectively priceless artefact was transited across the Channel in secret in July. Prime Minister Burnham, who took office six weeks ago, called the tapestry's return "a landmark moment" in the history of the two countries. He also hailed ties with Macron's French government more generally in the House of Commons on Wednesday, alluding to reduced illegal migration crossings of the English Channel — a bid to counter one of Reform UK's favorite summer talking points. "The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation — the same cooperation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low," Burnham said. It's Macron's first UK visit since Burnham took office and their first in-person meeting as leaders. What is the Bayeux Tapestry? The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066. Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration. This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millenium, and turned out to be the last one for a millenium. The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language. The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy. Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.33
New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week. This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9. What happened in the parliamentary ceremony? Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo. House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath. "I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said. Queen Mette-Marit skips event amid complications following lung transplant Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending. She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June. In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday. "As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said. What's the role of Norway's largely symbolic monarchy? Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century. When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite. Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first. Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

item.title: Nepal: Two pulled alive from tunnel nine days after floods
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.27
Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after catastrophic floods swept through the country's border region with China. Emergency teams are continuing efforts to reach hundreds more believed trapped inside similar tunnels. The men, identified as mechanical foreman Sanjay Shah and mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan, were freed from the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station's tunnel along the Trishuli River, according to a statement from the office of Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha. "As long as there is breath, there is hope!" Shrestha said in a statement. "Rescue operations are continuing in all the affected tunnels. Let everyone's efforts and prayers continue. We have not lost hope." What do we know about the rescue? Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning, authorities said. Video and photos showed Maharjan, 45, pulled from a hole in the ground as bystanders cheered. Images showed him being placed on a stretcher, while Shah, 30, whose face was covered in mud, was carried out on a worker's back to a rescue tent, where army doctors fitted him with an oxygen mask and checked his vitals. An aide to the energy minister said Maharjan could not move his hands or legs, while Shah's injuries were not considered critical. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Family members reacted with relief. Amir Maharjan, Kabir's brother, told the Associated Press, "I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," adding that the family was heading to the hospital to see him. What is happening at the hydropower project sites? These were the first successful rescues concerning the hydropower projects along the Trishuli River. Officials say as many as 900 workers remain missing across a number of project sites, with roughly 500 believed trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities. At the Trishuli 3A project specifically, the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal put the number of missing workers at 557, with about 115 believed trapped in the main tunnel. Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials remained hopeful more survivors would be found: "We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people," he said. A team of experts coordinating through a WhatsApp group has been guiding rescue crews at the sites, becoming a key tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery in the search effort. What is the scale of damage caused by the Nepal floods? Separately, Nepal's disaster authority estimated the floods caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.56 billion, €2.20 billion) in damage to property, housing and infrastructure, Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told Reuters. He said the first four months of early recovery — including rebuilding roads, setting up temporary shelters, and restoring water and power — would cost an estimated $52.6 million. "These are estimated amounts. We have calculated this in coordination with different concerned agencies and departments," Upreti said, noting a more detailed assessment would follow. He said Nepal would need to rebuild around 20,000 houses in flood-affected areas, with at least 7,500 destroyed outright. The floods on August 26 were triggered by the collapse of a glacier upstream on the Trishuli River that sent a wall of ice, rock and mud through towns and villages near the Nepal-China border. At least 1,259 people have been killed in Nepal, according to the country's disaster management agency, with more than 5,000 still missing. China reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing on the Tibet side of the border as of late Wednesday. Edited by: Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Germany, partners aim to finalize 'return hubs' by year end
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.18
Germany and other European Union countries are aiming to finalize so-called "return hubs," detention centers outside the bloc where they wish to send migrants whose asylum requests have been rejected, by the end of the year. The European Parliament in June approved tougher migration rules that paved the way for the creation of "return hubs." "We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year," which would then enable the establishment of so-called "return hubs," said German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt after a meeting with his counterparts from Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands in Copenhagen on Friday. He added that "technical discussions" were currently underway with countries outside the EU, but did not name such countries. What did the EU ministers say on 'return hubs?' The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the "return hubs." Uganda and Rwanda in particular are seen as possibilities —two autocratically ruled countries. "Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union," said Danish Migrations Minister Morten Bodskov. Both the Greek and Danish migration ministers said they wished for the "return hubs" to become operational by 2027. "We do not accept that foreigners staying illegally in Denmark should be rewarded because of our difficulties in returning them," Bodskov said in an earlier statement. The controversial scheme had already been briefly adopted by the United Kingdom under the former conservative government, but has since been scrapped after the social democratic Labour Party came to power. In Italy, the right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni reached a similar deal with Albania which currently faces legal challenges. Are EU 'return hubs' legal? The legality of the plans for the so-called "return hubs" remains unclear under EU law. A legal appraisal issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in April concluded that the controversial Italian deportation centers in Albania do not violate European law. EU law does not in principle prohibit member states from establishing such centers outside their own territory. However, it stipulates that deportees continue to receive legal counsel and linguistic support, and are able to maintain contact with their families and the relevant authorities. Andreas Grünewald, a migration expert with the German evangelical charity Brot für die Welt (Bread for the World), questioned the feasibility of the plans, calling them "practically difficult to implement and highly problematic in terms of human rights." He said ministers risked running into "political dead ends." Rights organizations criticize EU 'return hubs' The highly controversial plan has been met with wide rejection from rights groups, including children's charities and church organizations, who have criticized the plans for what they see as the "criminalization of migration." Marta Welander from the International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global humanitarian aid, relief and development NGO, said the plans risk "normalizing detainment in prison-like facilities" and warned that deportees may face "persecution, torture or worse" in their destination countries. Caritas, a Catholic charity operating in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Slovakia, said that migrants risked becoming trapped in a "legal grey area" if "arbitrarily and indefinitely detained" in the hubs. Florian Westphal, CEO of Save The Children Germany, warned of the risks faced in particular by children and young people. "The planned return centers in third countries are places of uncertainty and carry the risk of massive violations of children's rights," he said. "Transferring children to states with which they have no connection, and where they face the risk of deprivation of liberty and are cut off from key figures in their lives, cannot be in their best interests. Children deserve unconditional protection, no matter where they come from or where they live." Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.04
On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage. On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators. In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received. While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals. Already 160 attacks on critical infrastructure this year What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors. Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year. People in Berlin express concern over Russia Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin. One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?" One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening." A freeze in German-Russian relations The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4. The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years. "We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year. The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war. Germany's support for Ukraine as a motive? Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe. Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it. He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure." At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war. Private firms urged to strengthen infrastructure security But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists. A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS," aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force. Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police. As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection." Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves. "Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said. What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest. This article was translated from German.

item.title: German company successfully launches rocket to space
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.04
A Spectrum space rocket built by German company Isar Aerospace was launched into space from the Norwegian spaceport at Andoya. "We're in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company wrote on X. "Germany has spaceflight capabilities," said the country's Ministry for Research, Technology and Space on X, praising a "milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise". This was the German company's second attempt to launch the Spectrum rocket into space. The first attempt, which took place 18 months ago, was unsuccessful. What is Spectrum rocket? The Spectrum rocket is designed for small and medium-sized payloads. It carried five smal satellites and an in-flight technological experiment, the company said. According to Isar Aerospace, the launch was for "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload." The move is believed to bring Europe closer to being able to offer satellite flights from its own territory. Several countries voiced interest in the growing market of commercial space missions, including Britain and Sweden. In March, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the launch site of Isar, a Bavaria-based company, showing support for its efforts and for European autonomy at a time when the world order is changing under US President Donald Trump. Isar is also working on the development of a second launch site, located in Canada. The company said that while the US launched 198 rockets last year, Europe's tally was just eight. Isar's goal is to produce some 40 rockets a year. Competition includes SpaceX Although the rocket is not yet ready for mass production, Isar has already received orders through 2028. The Spectrum rocket is intended to send both civilian and military satellites into low Earth orbit, meaning a few hundred kilometers above the Earth's surface. The industry includes Elon Musk's SpaceX and ArianeGroup, a French joint venture between Airbus and Safran that operates a spaceport in French Guiana, located in South America. For the sake of developing new rockets and extend its testing and launch infrastructure, Isar said last week it received €200 million ($232 million) from the European Space Agency (ESA). Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Indonesia: Flights canceled as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.97
Hundreds of flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday morning, more than 150 kilometers (93 miles) away. The volcano produced a fountain of lava and loud sounds heard up to 700 kilometers away, Indonesia's geological agency said in a statement. The cloud of ash was detected up to a height of 6,000 meters (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano and a plume of up to 15,000 meters on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG posted on its website. No incidents of casualties were reported, and no evacuation orders were issued. The closest township is more than 16 kilometers away, but the authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers from the volcano's active crater. Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned. Indonesia cancels flights The ash spread across parts of the capital Jakarta and Lampung province on the southern tip of Sumatra island, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said. Authorities have suspended operations at six airports following eruptions from Mount Anak Krakatoa, the ministry said. "The Husein Sastranegara Airport in Bandung showed indications of being affected. Consequently, we have declared... the airport closed to flights," Dudy Purwagandhi told a press conference Sunday, mentioning the latest airport to be shuttered. Operations at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the country's largest and in the capital, Jakarta, were suspended earlier. Soekarno-Hatta International Airport posted on Instagram that it had suspended flight operations until 9:30 a.m. (0230 GMT) due to volcanic ash. "Due to increased activity from the Mount Anak Krakatau eruption, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has temporarily suspended flight operations from 5:30 a.m. to 9.30 a.m.," the airport said. The disruption of flight operations has impacted more than 22,000 passengers, the transport ministry said in a statement, adding that 209 flights were affected, particularly to and from Singapore. Anak Krakatau lies in the middle between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia's vast island chain, which sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire," where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are frequent. Anak Krakatau means "Child of Krakatau." The volcano is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental eruption in 1883 triggered a period of global cooling.
