item.title: The End of American Sanctuary
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.44
Among its many advantages, the United States benefits from a rare form of geographic luck: it is bracketed on the east and west by two vast moats, the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, and on the north and south by only two neighbors, both of whom are relatively friendly. Adding to this good fortune is that, since the end of World War II, the United States has possessed a powerful nuclear arsenal and unparalleled military, economic, and technological might. Despite the 9/11 terrorist attacks, this mix of geography, deterrence, and power has led many Americans to feel almost untouchable at home. According to a 2024 Chicago Council on Global Affairs poll, just 19 percent of those surveyed expressed concern about foreign threats. It is time for Americans to revise their assumptions. In fact, the U.S. homeland has never been as vulnerable to attack as it is today. China, Russia, and North Korea are building up their conventional and nuclear capabilities to strike the United States across a variety of domains—and U.S. defenses have not kept pace. A major evolution in technology and tactics, meanwhile, has increased the threat of subversion and gray-zone attacks: drones from state and nonstate actors can strike almost any target in the United States, and adversaries such as China can conduct AI-enabled offensive cyber-operations that can destroy or damage critical infrastructure. The United States is not prepared. The country’s air and missile defenses are porous. Arcane domestic laws and policies prevent the necessary coordination and authority to defend against drone attacks. And energy, water, financial, health-care, and other infrastructure remain vulnerable to advanced cyberattacks. Faced with these new threats, federal, state, and local entities in the United States are caught flat-footed. The 9/11 attacks happened in part because of policymakers’ inability to grasp that the world was changing and to share information across government agencies that could have protected the country. Without an overhaul of the nation’s homeland security apparatus, Washington is in danger of making this mistake again. MISSILES OVER THE MOAT Security measures enacted after September 11 were designed to protect the U.S. homeland from terrorism. The U.S.A. Patriot Act and subsequent legislation enabled U.S. agencies to collect more intelligence at home and abroad. The Department of Homeland Security, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the National Counterterrorism Center, and the Joint Terrorism Task Forces were created or enhanced to better share intelligence about terrorism and other threats. The FBI significantly expanded the number of Joint Terrorism Task Forces across the country, coordinated with state and local law enforcement, and conducted intelligence-led operations to identify and arrest terrorists. These measures were helpful at the time, when terrorism was the biggest threat to the U.S. homeland. And they were successful in preventing the vast majority of terrorist plots in the homeland. But today, some of the greatest threats to the United States come from state actors. China, Russia, and North Korea all possess intercontinental missiles capable of hitting the U.S. homeland—and all have conducted tests and exercises to show that they are capable of using them. The wars in Iran and Ukraine suggest that possessing a nuclear arsenal, even one as large as the U.S. arsenal, no longer protects against conventional attacks on the homeland as it once did. Iran and its network of proxy forces have lobbed tens of thousands of rockets, missiles, and drones at major population centers in Israel. Ukraine has successfully struck Russian cities, energy infrastructure, industrial base targets, logistics nodes, and military bases without incurring a nuclear response from the Kremlin. Advanced Israeli and Russian air and missile defense systems have struggled to stop these drones and missile attacks. In the event of a conventional attack on U.S. soil, American air and missile defense systems might, too. The United States lacks sufficient numbers of air defense systems and interceptors to protect against ballistic missiles. The war with Iran has reduced the military’s global supply of THAAD interceptors by as much as 80 percent and Patriot interceptors by as much as 50 percent. In addition, homeland defense against cruise missiles remains porous. Cruise missiles are difficult to defend against. They fly close to the earth in order to stay below conventional radar, and they use mountains, valleys, and hills to hide from ground-based sensors—what is called “terrain masking.” The United States does not have enough missile defense systems in enough areas to protect against cruise missiles. China especially has expanded and updated its ability to strike the United States. In addition to missiles, the threat from China now extends into space. China can strike targets in the U.S. homeland using a Fractional Orbital Bombardment System, which places a warhead flying at hypersonic speed into low-earth orbit, allowing it to approach the U.S. homeland from an unpredictable direction and bypass traditional early warning radar and missile defense networks. The People’s Liberation Army is also researching other space-based capabilities, such as orbital strike weapons, which would theoretically strike the U.S. homeland by dropping projectiles from space. CHEAP SHOTS The U.S. homeland is also facing novel subversion threats. State and nonstate actors have long used physical sabotage against critical infrastructure, disinformation, and offensive cyber-operations to weaken their adversaries below the threshold of conventional warfare. But new technologies and tactics, including AI, present new challenges for the United States. Drones are the most obvious example. Technological advances have already made drones cheaply and readily available for purchase, with longer ranges, higher payloads, and an improved ability to evade electronic warfare. Adversaries may soon be able to fly drones in coordinated swarms using AI, effectively overwhelming any defenses. Allies and adversaries alike are now engaged in an arms race, ramping up drone production and use in an attempt to innovate their way to the cutting edge. Russia is producing as many as seven million weaponized drones per year. According to some estimates, China has the capacity to build one billion drones per year. It wouldn’t take that much, however, to wreak havoc on the U.S. homeland. In 2025, Ukraine smuggled over 100 drones into Russia inside cargo trucks to conduct strikes that damaged or destroyed roughly one-third of Russia’s active bomber fleet and caused approximately $7 billion in damages. Operation Spider’s Web was a spectacular success for Ukrainian forces—and a chilling reminder of the United States’ susceptibility to a similar attack. An adversary could conceal weaponized drones inside modified cargo vans, shipping containers, or trucks with slidable roofs and position the vehicles near high-value targets, such as military airfields or naval bases, without detection. They could program the drones to launch simultaneously using commercial cellular networks, circumventing domestic air defense and signal-jamming measures and effectively bypassing strategic early warning radar systems. According to some estimates, China has the capacity to build one billion drones per year. Such an attack on U.S. soil might seem far-fetched. But unauthorized drone incursions on U.S. military installations, nuclear power plants, and other critical infrastructure—not to mention outdoor concert venues, sports stadiums, transportation infrastructure, and ports—have been increasing over the past several years. In March, for example, Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, which houses long-range B-52 bombers, went into lockdown after numerous unauthorized drones were spotted hovering over sensitive areas of the base. In June, the FBI arrested five suspects in an alleged plot to target the Ultimate Fighting Championship event on the White House South Lawn with explosive-laden drones. Artificial intelligence makes individual drones and swarms of drones harder to stop because they do not rely on remote radio signals that can be jammed by electronic countermeasures. Drones are not the only problem made worse by AI’s rapid development. Agentic AI systems such as Anthropic’s Mythos will make it far easier for state and nonstate adversaries, such as terrorists, to penetrate cyberdefenses and attack critical infrastructure at a scale never before possible. Once directed, AI agents can discover flaws in corporate and government computer systems and execute self-directed cyberattacks with minimal human oversight. Even before the advent of these AI systems, the shockingly poor state of national and municipal cyberdefenses made American critical infrastructure an inviting target. Beginning in 2021, China’s Volt Typhoon attacks infiltrated U.S. power grids, water treatment plants, telecommunication systems, and transportation hubs, embedding malware that could sabotage them in the event of a U.S.-Chinese crisis. An AI-enabled Volt Typhoon operation would allow attackers to shift from a slow, human-enabled campaign that takes months or years to a nearly instantaneous, self-adapting campaign against numerous targets simultaneously that could be vastly more damaging. Finally, beyond drones and AI, there is the growing threat of direct-ascent antisatellite weapons, which are missiles launched from the ground, sea, or air that travel into space to strike and destroy a satellite in orbit, as well as directed-energy weapons and electronic warfare systems that can target U.S. satellites in low-earth orbit and geosynchronous orbit. China and Russia are actively developing and testing a broad range of antisatellite and other counterspace weapons. If implemented, such space-based attacks could degrade GPS and navigation, ground commercial flights, and disrupt logistics networks that rely on satellite tracking for freight. In other words, they could at least temporarily grind daily life in the United States to a halt. IMAGINING THE UNIMAGINABLE To better prepare for an attack on the homeland, Washington needs first to fortify the active defenses that protect the country’s critical infrastructure. It needs to build and deploy more upper-range systems like Patriot and THAAD for ballistic missiles, medium-range systems such as the Indirect Fire Protection Capability system for cruise missiles, and short-range systems such as the Coyote and Merops systems to counter drones. Directed-energy weapons—such as high-energy lasers and high-power microwave systems—and radio-frequency jamming and electronic warfare systems are also useful to defend against drone attacks. The United States needs more systems to defend critical infrastructure, as well as training for personnel. It should also ramp up passive defenses, such as digging underground facilities for vital infrastructure and placing high-density and layered concrete barriers around ground systems, power-generation units, ammunition storage facilities, and barracks. Since it would be exorbitantly expensive to protect everything in the homeland, Washington should initially focus on reinforcing critical bases and infrastructure that China or other adversaries could target in a conflict. Key locations include military command-and-control facilities, bomber bases, nuclear weapons sites, air and missile defense systems, and major naval bases. Golden Dome, the Trump administration’s proposed homeland air and missile defense system, can play an important role in this effort. The plan aims to create a unified command-and-control network of sensors, weapons, and other systems to detect and shoot down incoming drones and missiles. But Golden Dome is underfunded and has been slow to get off the ground. Moving forward, the U.S. priority should be accelerating plans to stitch together existing capabilities—not developing new ones—such as the U.S. military’s missile warning satellites; global network of radars and sensors; 44 ground-based interceptors in California and Alaska; and other federal, state, local, and commercial systems. The U.S. military also needs to ramp up live-fire exercises to test Golden Dome’s software and ability to detect, track, and hit incoming threats. Drones present a thornier problem. Commanders at military bases and personnel protecting critical infrastructure often do not have the legal authority to destroy or degrade drones that illegally fly into their airspace. Some recent laws, including the Safer Skies Act of 2025, grant state and local agencies (though not private-sector entities) greater license to detect and track hostile drones. But more comprehensive legislation is needed that allows operators who have received training to deploy and use counterdrone systems under federal or state and local law enforcement supervision. To mitigate the risk that newly empowered operators of counterdrone systems accidentally jam or shoot down civilian aircraft, more state and local personnel should be trained at the National Counter-UAS Training Center in Huntsville, Alabama. The United states can no longer rely on its geography and its nuclear arsenal to protect it. Intelligence sharing among federal, state, and local intelligence agencies improved after 9/11 to disrupt terrorist networks and foil planned attacks. But the evolving nuclear and conventional capabilities of China, Russia, and North Korea, as well as emerging tactics and technology such as drones and AI, make the intelligence practices of the “war on terror” largely obsolete. What’s more, self-inflicted wounds have damaged the few agencies well suited for today’s threats. The Trump administration, for example, has gutted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which oversees cyberdefenses and elections security. The United States needs to establish a robust National Counterintelligence Center, much like the National Counterterrorism Center it established after 9/11, that brings together analysts from multiple agencies to fuse intelligence, analyze threats, and coordinate strategic planning against Chinese, Iranian, Russian, and other threats to the homeland. At the state and local level, the Joint Terrorism Task Forces and Fusion Centers need to shift their focus and resources to tracking state-based threats to the homeland. Finally, the threats currently facing the U.S. homeland require a fundamental shift in mindset. U.S. policymakers, the country’s security establishment, and its citizens must recognize that the United States is in a new era; it can no longer rely on its geography and its nuclear arsenal to protect it. Finland, Israel, and Ukraine have long traditions of developing strategic plans and communicating to their publics about homeland threats. The United States should follow suit by educating the American public about the evolving threats to the homeland and developing a national resilience plan—much as Finland has done—to harden critical infrastructure, closely collaborate with the private sector, adapt laws, and communicate with the public. Americans’ overwhelming sense of safety was briefly and tragically shaken by the attacks on September 11, 2001, and the 9/11 Commission went on to argue that the United States faced a “generational challenge” from terrorist groups. A quarter century later, there is a new generation of Americans and a new generational challenge. If the 9/11 attacks were in large measure a failure of imagination and implementation, as the commission wrote, Washington risks repeating that same mistake today. item.title: The End of Thailand’s Long Stalemate?
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.42
For more than 25 years, Thailand’s conservative establishment and opposition forces have been locked in a struggle for the soul of the country. Royalists want palace institutions insulated from public criticism, a military licensed to intervene in times of political crisis, deferential political parties and politicians, and free rein to clamp down on political actors who fail to toe the line. The opposition calls for a constitutional monarchy, a military that stays in the barracks, a competitive party system responsive to the people’s wishes, and predictable checks and balances that do not unduly punish elected politicians. More often than not, the royalists have had the upper hand. They have mobilized protest movements, staged military coups, and banned opposition parties to prevent troublesome politicians from instituting changes that could limit their power and privileges. Yet every attempt to strike a decisive blow against the opposition has failed. Conservatives have not translated legal or extralegal victories into lasting governments. Opposition movements, meanwhile, have consistently reinvented themselves. Thaksin Shinawatra, the larger-than-life former policeman and telecom billionaire, built up enormous power as prime minister in the early 2000s, incurring the disdain of royalists. And even after a military coup removed Thaksin from the premiership in 2006, his parties remained electoral juggernauts. A yet more alarming challenge emerged on the horizon after a 2014 coup ousted Thaksin’s sister, Yingluck Shinawatra, from government: youth-based mass protests calling for reform of the monarchy in 2020 and progressive political parties who appealed to these younger voters. A stalemate had prevailed over Thai politics, with neither side able to overpower the other fully. That changed in February 2026, when Bhumjaithai, a low-profile party previously known primarily for campaigning to legalize cannabis, swept into power in national elections. With the implicit backing of the monarchy and the conservative establishment, Bhumjaithai has seized control of the Thai state, giving rise to a new mode of politics capable of both suppressing progressive forces in favour of cozy collaboration among elites and winning a general election without overt manipulation. Far from an electoral anomaly, the rise of Bhumjaithai is the culmination of a long effort by conservatives to retake the levers of power. In fact, the formerly also-ran party’s February triumph was part of a methodical, behind-the-scenes campaign to commandeer the state’s nominally neutral apparatuses, including its Senate and Constitutional Court. The alliance between the monarchical network and Bhumjaithai is more a marriage of convenience than a shared ideological project, and it may not last indefinitely. But shallow as it may be, it has already succeeded in decisively strengthening the conservative position, disempowering the major rival parties that threaten elite control, and potentially remaking the Thai state for years to come. RAINBOW COALITIONS The origins of Thailand’s current political order date back to 1997, when a group of elite liberal royalists, claiming a mandate from civil society, introduced a landmark new charter. Often referred to as “the people’s constitution,” it was a reaction to a disastrous military coup in 1991 and its bloody aftermath, including the deadly suppression of unarmed protesters in May 1992. The reforms aimed to coup-proof the political system by introducing checks and balances to prevent elected politicians from abusing their power and facilitate a smooth royal succession. It established an electoral commission, a constitutional court, an anticorruption agency, and a human rights commission, as well as a fully elected, purportedly nonpartisan Senate. The project backfired. It failed to stabilize Thai politics—probably an unrealistic goal to begin with—and the new parliamentary system allowed for the election of Thaksin as prime minister in 2001. A charismatic figure with populist authoritarian tendencies, he successfully mobilized lower-income voters in the heavily populated north and northeast regions of Thailand, melding them into an unbeatable electoral bloc. He used his considerable personal wealth, his party’s parliamentary dominance, and his bureaucratic connections to create a startlingly successful political machine. Thaksin bought off the Senate and the independent agencies, defanging them as neutral bodies, and installed loyalists in crucial posts intended to check the prime minister’s power. The country’s traditional elites were deeply threatened by Thaksin’s ascendance. The so-called Yellow Shirt movement, which appropriated a royal color, sought to make Thailand ungovernable. Through mass street protests and the occupation of public spaces and buildings, it paralyzed opposition rule three times: in 2006, 2008, and in 2013–14. But for all its success in ousting opposition-led governments, the Yellow Shirt movement never solved a basic problem: conservatives could bring down an elected government, but they couldn’t win an election to replace it. Conservatives were unable to tolerate ambitious, independent-minded administrations. The 2006 and 2014 political crises initially followed a similar pattern. Street protests destabilized and delegitimized Shinawatra-led governments, and military coups then removed them. Each time, the establishment brought in the Royal Thai Army to reorganize politics, rewrite the constitution, and reconfigure the party system in its favor before holding fresh elections. But military force failed to bring about durable conservative rule. Coups were short-term fixes that gradually eroded the legitimacy of the establishment. The Thai public was willing to tolerate only short interludes of military rule, and coup makers had no choice but to promise the imminent restoration of democracy. Generals, however, were bad at politics. The public quickly tired of them, and voters soon welcomed back the same kinds of politicians that soldiers had kicked out. In the 2007 elections, the first called by the ruling junta after the 2006 coup, for instance, Thaksin’s party was voted back into power. The experience was imprinted on the minds of conservatives when they launched the 2014 coup; the new government postponed elections until 2019. The inability of conservatives to break the opposition once and for all persuaded the establishment to try to cut deals with Thaksin’s Pheu Thai Party instead. A strategy of conciliation permitted the opposition to front a government as long as party leaders concentrated on managing the economy and did not challenge the special status of the monarchy. Pheu Thai, conservatives believed, could always be co-opted or browbeaten into a politics of benefit sharing in which wealth and power were divided between a Pheu Thai figurehead and conservative power brokers. This was the deal behind Yingluck Shinawatra’s administration of 2011 to 2014, an arrangement that both conservatives and Thaksin supporters found unsatisfying and were reluctant to acknowledge. But government by veto was inherently unstable. Eventually, the conservatives were unable to tolerate ambitious, independent-minded Pheu Thai administrations and brought them crashing down, as they did in the 2014 military coup. Where they did not want to use force, they turned to lawfare to limit the opposition’s power. Starting in 2019, a series of more progressive “orange” opposition parties proved wildly popular, especially among younger voters. After the orange Move Forward Party won the largest number of seats in Thailand’s National Assembly in the 2023 elections, the military-appointed Senate blocked its leader, Pita Limjaroenrat, from assuming the premiership. The following year, Move Forward was summarily dissolved—the fifth major opposition party to meet this fate—and the Constitutional Court banned Pita from political office for ten years. By 2025, the establishment was running out of options to disempower the opposition. Challenged by both pro-Thaksin forces and progressive orange parties, its old methods—military coups, dodgy deals, party bans, the judicial removal of prime ministers—were wearing thin. Conservatives desperately needed an alliance with a reliably deferential party that could win elections. HOLLOW PARTY Enter Bhumjaithai, a previously medium-sized party based in the northeastern province of Buriram. The product of a breakaway by a faction of members of parliament and former ministers from Thaksin’s party in 2008, Bhumjaithai had for the first 17 years of its existence no popular politicians among its ranks, no clear economic policies, and no national following. Yet under the guidance of the shadowy Newin Chidchob, Bhumjaithai has gradually become a force in Thai politics and a crucial ally of the monarchy and its sympathizers. Known euphemistically by the party faithful as “the school principal,” Newin served as a junior minister under Thaksin and in other governments but stepped back from frontline politics two decades ago, ostensibly to concentrate on building up his Buriram United soccer team. He neither grants interviews nor appears in public but exercises tight control over Bhumjaithai’s strategy and personnel. Current Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, a U.S.-trained engineer and former deputy minister whose family owns the massive Sino-Thai Engineering and Construction company, has served as the party’s leader and public face since 2012. What Newin and Anutin lack in ideological vision, they have made up for in strategic cunning, accumulating power wherever possible and making themselves useful to the monarchical network. Correctly diagnosing the establishment’s desperate need for a reliable political party with which to collaborate, they set out to distinguish their party from other conservative contenders, which were typically packed with reliable but often underperforming former bureaucrats. To do so, Newin and Anutin transformed Bhumjaithai into a major vehicle for influential provincial business interests. Control of the key ministries was a crucial first step in the project to capture state power. As a precondition to joining coalition governments as a junior partner, Bhumjaithai demanded ministerial positions that would help it secure stronger local networks. In 2019, Anutin became minister of public health and subsequently boosted the pay of over one million health volunteers in villages across the country. Anutin’s support turned many of them into canvassers for Bhumjaithai—an electoral masterstroke, given that Thai elections are often won and lost in these provincial areas, where vote-canvasser networks are all-important. Then, in 2023, Bhumjaithai secured control of the powerful Ministry of Interior, which oversees local governance in Thailand, including more than 70,000 village headmen. In the right hands, the Interior Ministry can be a formidable patronage machine, exerting authority over everything from local budgets to Senate elections. The party then combined the health and headmen networks to penetrate every community in Thailand. Today, Anutin still holds the post of interior minister, in addition to his position as prime minister. Other behind-closed-doors moves solidified Bhumjaithai’s power. For most Thai citizens, the selection of 200 new senators in 2024 through an arcane and untested self-nomination system barely registered, creating ample opportunity for manipulation. Candidates linked to Bhumjaithai gamed the system and secured around two-thirds of the supposedly neutral upper chamber—a majority that has allowed conservative forces to quietly block independent-minded candidates for the Constitutional Court, the Election Commission, and the Anticorruption Commission and to exercise veto power over any future changes to the constitution. Missteps by the opposition also smoothed the path for the party’s ultimate takeover of the state. When the Bhumjaithai-controlled Constitutional Court removed Thaksin’s daughter, Paetongtarn Shinawatra, as prime minister in August 2025, the orange party—now known as the People’s Party—voted for Anutin, rather than another Pheu Thai member, to replace her. People’s Party leaders naively believed a Bhumjaithai government would be in office for only a brief period and that after winning an early election, progressive forces could push to amend the constitution and reduce the entrenched power of the elite. This was a disastrous miscalculation. In the February election, Bhumjaithai shocked most observers by decisively topping the polls, winning 192 seats to the People’s Party’s 120 seats. With Bhumjaithai in control of both the internal levers of power and parliament, the prospects for progressive constitutional reform evaporated. SAME AS IT EVER WAS? By neutralizing the Pheu Thai and the People’s Party, Bhumjaithai has made itself the most successful conservative party in modern Thai history. Far from transforming the country’s politics, however, this dominance has ground it to a halt. The incarnation of transactional conservatism, Bhumjaithai now controls every major mechanism of the state. But whereas in the past the various royalist and opposition factions jockeying for influence each stood for something tangible, the party is a cipher, favored by many conservatives, yet largely devoid of ideological or policy content or an organic base of support. Today, a country known for mobilizing millions of people around big ideas, both during hotly contested elections and through massive extraparliamentary movements, is led by a party with no apparent ideas at all. The political reform project that began in the 1990s has run its course. So, too, have Thaksin’s project to empower the disadvantaged, the military’s nationalist project to restore order and defend the monarchy, and the progressive project to transform Thailand into a more open and equal place. At the same time, Bhumjaithai’s vacuous opportunism reflects a new form of realpolitik that appears much more durable than previous iterations. Royalists have grudgingly rallied around the party because they have nowhere else to go. Thaksin, recently chastened by an eight-month prison term, has gone quiet. Progressives criticize and deconstruct what they decry as the “blue regime” (after the color of Bhumjaithai’s logo) but struggle to articulate a realistic strategy to challenge it. Despite the contradictions that underpin Anutin’s government, it has shown no sign of imminent collapse. This hollow dominance has yielded a strange impasse. For the last six months, Anutin’s administration has mostly treaded water, postponing major initiatives. That impasse may not hold as younger generations become a force in Thai politics. Indeed, conservatives’ grip on power remains deeply contested and contingent. A united opposition that puts aside the long-standing differences between pro-Thaksin and progressive forces could in theory topple Bhumjaithai at the ballot box. A return to Move Forward’s winning slogan in 2023—a Thailand that is “not the same as before,” code for the dismantling of gerontocracy and unearned privilege across the country’s creaking structures and institutions—could serve as the basis for an alternative administration. But even if an anti-Bhumjaithai coalition were to take back power, it would struggle to unwind the party’s control of Thailand’s political institutions. However long Bhumjaithai’s present tenure in Bangkok lasts, that takeover of the levers of state power will be its enduring legacy. item.title: What 6 Different Versions of This Sex Comedy Say About the Countries That Made Them
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 6.22
Some fears transcend language, transcend cultures. The howl of a wolf, the scream of a hawk, or the doorbell ring of neighbors you invited over but now wish would go away. The uncanny mix of attraction, resentment, jealousy, and annoyance felt toward those we only hear through floorboards and glimpse in elevators is at the center of the droll apartment farce The Invite. The low-budget comedy debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and, thanks to good word of mouth, emerged as an unexpected summer hit alongside special effects blockbusters like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. It is now available to stream in North America, and as you’ll see, it’s a tale that echoes around the world. Some fears transcend language, transcend cultures. The howl of a wolf, the scream of a hawk, or the doorbell ring of neighbors you invited over but now wish would go away. The uncanny mix of attraction, resentment, jealousy, and annoyance felt toward those we only hear through floorboards and glimpse in elevators is at the center of the droll apartment farce The Invite. The low-budget comedy debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and, thanks to good word of mouth, emerged as an unexpected summer hit alongside special effects blockbusters like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey. It is now available to stream in North America, and as you’ll see, it’s a tale that echoes around the world. The Invite takes place over one night and is set almost entirely in one location—a desirable-but-not-ostentatious San Francisco apartment in a sonically porous building. The apartment is owned by a jaded music instructor who has abandoned his rock star dreams (we learn he inherited the pad from his parents) played by Seth Rogen, and his deeply unhappy wife played by Olivia Wilde (who is also the director of the film). There’s an early-teens daughter in the mix, but she’s luckily away for the night, so Wilde’s character has sprung a surprise dinner party on her husband. The neighbors, the ones they talk about constantly, are coming over. The ongoing spousal chatter, which is partially a source of shared humor but mostly a wellspring of deeply held animus, comes from the upstairs couple’s regular and thunderous lovemaking sessions—a matrimonial hobby we’ll soon learn the downstairs couple have long since quit. The upstairs duo is played by Edward Norton, a kind but devilish firefighter, and Spanish actor Penélope Cruz, a ravishing, earthy therapist who exudes continental sophistication and excitement. In short time, the downstairs couple reveal themselves to be a bickering, miserable mess, but they briefly put aside their sniping when the upstairs couple shares that they are swingers, and the sleep-depriving sounds come from group sex adventures with a revolving door of participants. As the evening continues, the titular invite comes—would Rogen and Wilde’s characters, neurotic sourpusses though they may be, care to join Norton and Cruz’s for an intimate interlude? The movie is extremely funny, but also insightful and sad, thanks to a sharp screenplay by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones, as well as all four of the performances—especially Wilde, who skitters between debilitating insecurity, marital revulsion, and brazen lust, sometimes all within the same shot. She’s given life-or-death stakes to what could otherwise be a diverting filmed play, aided by rapid editing and a tension-rich original score by Devonté Hynes. The movie is a highwire act, and during the promotional cycle, she regularly cited the influence of Mike Nichols’ adaptation of Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, a key New Hollywood text. Wilde’s references to Nichols are certainly apt, but deviate from a more exact comparison: The Invite is a remake of a recent Spanish film, The People Upstairs (also called Sentimental), which writer-director Cesc Gay adapted from his own play. The People Upstairs came out in 2020 and between then and Wilde’s film’s release, there were four (yes, four) other versions of this story produced—in Switzerland, Italy, South Korea, and France. (A Belgian/Dutch version is en route.) While international remakes are not uncommon, I feel confident in saying that what’s happened with Gay’s work is unprecedented both in its speed and numbers. In the early days of “talking pictures,” one could sometimes find business-minded producers who would crank out alternates of a movie using the same sets and crew but (usually) different actors in different languages for foreign markets. Most of these iterations are now considered lost films, but several are notable. The all-star revue Paramount on Parade from 1930 holds the record with 13 different variants, including ones in Hungarian and Serbian. When Alfred Hitchcock shot Murder! in 1930, he stayed in the director’s chair for the German version, released as Mary in 1931. (He was used to this sort of thing, having filmed both the silent and talking versions of Blackmail in 1929.) Translations went the other way, too. An English version of Josef von Sternberg’s 1930 classic The Blue Angel starring Marlene Dietrich was considered lost for decades until a copy was found in a German archive and presented in 2009. The most celebrated example is George Melford’s Spanish-language Dracula from 1931, which was shot at night (spooky!) after Bela Lugosi and director Tod Browning left Universal’s stages. That English-language Dracula gave us iconic lines like “I never drink … wine,” and was, of course, an instant classic, but if you have hours to kill, I recommend visiting film snob message boards to see how many cinephiles are eager to argue that the Spanish Dracula is greatly superior. (I say they are both good!) But there’s a key difference between then and now. The profusion of versions of The People Upstairs does not represent a production entity looking to maximize profit. It is an organic recognition of a story with legs across different cultures. From a practical standpoint, one can see why local film industries, still wobbly from COVID safety protocols in the early part of this decade, would want to sink their teeth into a one-location movie with just four performers. Quick and easy. But those mechanics aside, what does it say about the world that so many of us are understood to be interested in sex-deprived married couples thunderstruck by their lustful neighbors? Of the six versions of this film that now exist, only the original Spanish and current Hollywood versions are easily found in North America. But leaping across borders is what we at Foreign Policy are all about. After many rounds of emails, Instagram DMs, and the deployment of some translation software, I am proud to say that I have seen each rendition. I immersed myself in this tale of would-be spouse-swapping hoping to learn more about specific cultures. Whether or not my discoveries are truly foundational to a national character is open to discussion, but pages and pages of notes show that this exercise was, if nothing else, fascinating. For starters, I now know that German-speaking Swiss are more into slapstick than I was previously aware, if Die Nachbarn von Oben (The Neighbors From Upstairs) director Sabine Boss is a true representative. Like Brahms interpreting Handel, some scenes of Cesc Gay’s original Spanish film only exist in the bones of each variation, but a few melodic lines remain constant. All six versions retain the reveal that the downstairs woman intentionally crosses her unshaded window while naked, knowing that the upstairs man is likely looking at her. Similarly, she urges her husband not to complain about the lovemaking upstairs because she is happy that the upstairs woman is having such aggressive orgasms—and Wilde is terrified that discussing it will ruin it for her. (This is played as a joke.) There’s also a big laugh across all six versions when the invitation comes, and the downstairs woman starts verbally going through her calendar, causing the downstairs man to complain that it isn’t normal to schedule an orgy. In the Hollywood version, Cruz’s exoticism comes from her Iberian origins, and she even brings over a flan. No other version makes her a foreigner, and in the Spanish, Swiss, and Italian versions, she makes an unspecified Indian dish that is spicy and (the upstairs man jokes) an aphrodisiac. In the French version, she makes “tapas,” and in the South Korean version, some kind of elaborate fried eggplant on a cake stand with a bow on it. Music comes up a lot. In the Hollywood film, the downstairs husband is a frustrated rock musician. In Spain and Switzerland, his repertoire is classical piano; in Italy, it is jazz. In South Korea, he’s not a musician at all, but a film director stuck in years of development on a television project he isn’t that enthusiastic about to begin with. The South Korean film (also called The People Upstairs) is the version with some of the bigger changes. For starters, the downstairs neighbors do not have kids or a pet. (The French version includes not just a daughter, but a pivotal dog.) Moreover, the upstairs sex-positive neighbors are deliberately cast as older and more conservatively dressed. Indeed, the upstairs woman looks like a newscaster and the upstairs man initially comes across as a bit of a dork, wearing a cardigan with ducks on it. Each version shows that the downstairs man has an office, but the South Korean spin strongly suggests that it functions as his nightly bedroom. There’s a gag in each film when the downstairs couple admits how long it has been since they last made love. Most versions, including the Rogen-Wilde version, say “about a year.” But the South Korean couple say four years. (The French version evades the question with, “I can’t even remember the last time.”) Indeed, the two ends of the sexuality spectrum are represented by South Korea and France. In every version, when the upstairs neighbors talk about their group sex encounters, they say they usually limit them to four to six people, except one time when there was 10 for someone’s birthday. (This builds to a variation of a “well, birthdays are special” joke.) The French version keeps this gag but doubles the number: There were 20 participants one New Year’s Eve, apparently. There’s also a funny moment where the upstairs neighbors talk about sexual boundaries and proclivities, with some versions getting more lewd than others. (Quite frankly, the Hollywood version may be the dirtiest of them all.) In multiple versions, the upstairs man declares that his partner is fond of anal sex, and she plain-facedly confirms it. But the South Korean version includes dialogue about enjoying sex “Korean style.” (Here I must tell you, reader, that I have no clue what this means. Furthermore, asking Google “what is Korean-style sex” did nothing but poison my algorithm such that I can no longer use my laptop at the public library. We’re just going to have to accept that not everything translates.) All six versions of the movie build to their conclusion by raising the stakes in different ways. Seth Rogen’s back gives out in the Hollywood version; in the Swiss film, there’s a piano on fire then drunken nakedness. The French version, however, has a wild twist: The off-screen daughter isn’t a preteen at a friend’s sleepover, but a 20-year-old who only comes back from school now and again. It is soon discovered that a particularly noisy night of lovemaking came from the upstairs man seducing her. (To his credit, he didn’t realize who she was.) While this leads to expected anger from the downstairs man, the upstairs woman is also upset—because she wasn’t involved. “We’re supposed to be libertines together!” she cries. (The downstairs woman, the mother of the seduced, isn’t too bothered by the story at all, for what it’s worth.) Across the six films, the story ends with the downstairs couple confronting the fact that their marriage has collapsed, and the next step—separation—is presented as a reasonable, maybe even happy, ending. The big question is whether or not they go through with it or stay in their rut. All versions are ambiguous. The Spanish, Swiss, and Italian versions suggest rapprochement. (I’ve barely mentioned the Italian version, simply called Neighbors, because it’s pretty boring—though it does feature the nicest apartment.) The French and Hollywood versions lean more toward a breakup, but suggest that, in deciding to do so, the couple will grow in maturity and maybe even deepen their friendship. The South Korean version is the true outlier—our younger couple downstairs seems to be quite happy, and maybe, just maybe, has gotten there thanks to their new hobby of swinging. If and when that version (called The People Upstairs, for future reference) ever becomes more widely available, you can watch it and judge for yourself. Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central New Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Moscow’s Moment of Global Summitry
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.30
Moscow’s Moment of Global Summitry The war in Ukraine may rage on, but Russia remains far from an international pariah. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Russia’s attendance at key international conferences, how renewed conflict in Iran sparked a global bond sell-off, and the fallout of Zambia’s disputed presidential election. The Kremlin Refuses to Be Sidelined Russian forces launched a sixth straight day of missile and drone strikes at the Ukrainian capital and its surrounding areas on Tuesday, killing at least 12 people in attacks that damaged residential homes. At the same time, several high-ranking Kremlin officials participated in a slew of global conferences focused on advancing Moscow’s economic and diplomatic agendas. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Russia’s attendance at key international conferences, how renewed conflict in Iran sparked a global bond sell-off, and the fallout of Zambia’s disputed presidential election. The Kremlin Refuses to Be Sidelined Russian forces launched a sixth straight day of missile and drone strikes at the Ukrainian capital and its surrounding areas on Tuesday, killing at least 12 people in attacks that damaged residential homes. At the same time, several high-ranking Kremlin officials participated in a slew of global conferences focused on advancing Moscow’s economic and diplomatic agendas. Russia’s ability to engage with the international community at the highest levels despite its continued war against Ukraine signals that Moscow has managed to avoid becoming the global pariah that many Western powers have advocated for. Nowhere was this more obvious than in Asheville, North Carolina, where U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov on Monday on the sidelines of the G-20 finance ministers’ meeting. This was the first time that Moscow’s top financial official attended the global gathering in person since the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022. Axios reported on Monday that the two officials discussed U.S. President Donald Trump’s Russia-Ukraine peace proposal, opportunities for economic growth, and G-20 engagement. Although Bessent reportedly ruled out economic relief for Russia while the war continues, many European countries were unhappy with Washington’s decision to invite the Kremlin. “We do not trust Russia,” Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told Reuters. “They lie constantly, and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them.” European Union economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis stressed that “we do not think now is the time to normalize Russia” or its presence at the G-20. And German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said he’d assured his European colleagues that he would not pose for a photo with the Russian finance minister. But Moscow refuses to be sidelined. The Kremlin also had a prominent presence at this week’s Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit, further cementing its partnerships with key U.S. allies and adversaries, including China, India, Pakistan, and Iran, and bolstering Moscow’s efforts to challenge Western hegemony on the world stage. On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin jointly signed the summit’s “Bishkek Declaration,” which condemns U.S. and Israeli military action against Iran and its proxies as well as denounces Western sanctions on some of the SCO’s members, including Russia. After the SCO summit, Russia then turned its attention to the Eastern Economic Forum. Hosted in the Russian city of Vladivostok, the conference welcomed delegations on Tuesday from 80 countries to discuss ways to foster greater trade among Asia-Pacific nations, attract foreign investment, and improve quality of life. Of the VIP guests, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s attendance signaled Russia’s growing interest in Southeast Asia. Today’s Most Read - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Yes, We’re in an AI Bubble. Just Look to 1980s Japan. by Howard W. French - Jordan Sees Bigger Threat From Israel Than Iran by Sean Yom What We’re Following Global bond sell-off. Government bond yields hit record highs on Tuesday, as renewed fighting between U.S. and Iranian forces reignited worldwide inflation concerns. Notably, Japan’s 10-year and two-year benchmarks jumped to 3 percent and 1.81 percent, respectively, for the first time since 1996. And in the United Kingdom, 10-year bonds rose more than 9 basis points to their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis. Germany and France also recorded significant government bond jumps. Economists point to ballooning government debts, high costs of living, and rising energy prices due to the Iran war as the main causes of the global bond sell-off. On Tuesday, Brent crude exceeded $92 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate reached more than $88 per barrel, and European natural gas prices reached their highest level since March. Speaking on the sidelines of the G-20 finance ministers’ meeting, Bessent tried to downplay the global bond sell-off and defend Washington’s decision to intervene in the market last month. “The U.S. bond market has been the best performing market since the president came in,” Bessent said. Yields on 30-year Treasuries are currently close to their highest level in 19 years. Inauguration amid arrests. Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in on Tuesday for a second, five-year term, following a disputed Aug. 13 election marred by a government-led crackdown against the opposition. Yet several African leaders—including Kenyan President William Ruto, Botswanan President Duma Boko, and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa—attended Hichilema’s inauguration, granting foreign support for the election’s results. While votes were still being counted on election night, security forces launched a raid on the home of Hichilema’s main challenger, Brian Mundubile, arresting 11 people that authorities claim were “in possession of high-grade military weapons, ammunition and other materials for use in armed insurrection.” Opposition party member and former Transportation Minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot during the operation. The raid forced Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, to go into hiding at a United Nations building. However, after Hichilema put pressure on the U.N. to turn them over, Mundubile and Zulu surrendered to police, upon which they were arrested on treason charges. On Aug. 18, Zambia’s electoral commission declared Hichilema the winner, with around 60 percent of the vote versus Mundubile’s roughly 38 percent. Mundubile rejected the results, citing alleged voting irregularities. But the courts would not accept Mundubile’s legal challenge, as they were sealed off from accepting petitions. Taipei’s seat at the table. China condemned Taiwan’s attendance on Tuesday at the Pacific Islands Forum, arguing that the island does not qualify for participation. “The Taiwan authorities sent [Taiwanese Foreign Minister] Lin Chia-lung and other Taiwan independence separatists to make sneaky visits around in a vain attempt to attract eyeballs and attention, and the result can only be inviting disgrace upon themselves,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. Qian Bo, China’s special envoy for Pacific Island affairs, added that “there will always be consequences” for Taiwan’s involvement. “It’s not a threat.” Beijing does not recognize Taipei’s sovereignty, and in recent years, it has made substantial headway in pressuring other Asia-Pacific nations to abandon diplomatic relations with Taiwan. Only three Pacific Island countries maintain formal ties with Taiwan: the Marshall Islands, Tuvalu, and Palau, the last of which is hosting this week’s summit. It is unclear what China’s threatened consequences might entail. However, the forum’s 18 permanent members appear committed to Taiwan’s involvement, which will include attendance at meetings and side events as a development partner. “The Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country,” Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday in response to China’s remarks. Odds and Ends It’s the end of an era. After leading Argentina to the 2026 FIFA World Cup final this summer, 39-year-old soccer star Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international soccer on Monday. “It was a decision that hurt—and still hurts deeply—but I understand that the time has come,” Messi wrote in a letter posted on Instagram. The letter was originally dated July 21, two days after the World Cup concluded, but Messi said he chose to hold off publishing it while his father suffered from health issues; his father, Jorge, died on Aug. 8. Messi’s 21-year legacy includes 207 games and 125 goals at the international level, making him the world’s No. 2 scorer behind longtime rival Cristiano Ronaldo. Messi will continue to play at club level with Inter Miami. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: The Novel Imagining Life After a Second Civil War
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.07
The Novel Imagining Life After a Second Civil War Emily St. John Mandel explores what follows U.S. collapse, plus more fiction in September. Domed cities—those classic symbols of science (and climate) fiction—make an appearance in both of the novels we’re reading this month, which transport readers to the United States after a second civil war and an eerie utopian community on a Greek island. Exit Party: A Novel Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf, 320 pp., $32, September 2026) Domed cities—those classic symbols of science (and climate) fiction—make an appearance in both of the novels we’re reading this month, which transport readers to the United States after a second civil war and an eerie utopian community on a Greek island. Exit Party: A Novel Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf, 320 pp., $32, September 2026) The United States is known as a country of relentless—and sometimes naive—optimism. So it’s striking that, in recent years, serious thinkers from across the political spectrum have taken to warning of the possibility of a second civil war, or some other form of U.S. societal collapse. In a stunning new novel, Emily St. John Mandel imagines what might come after that potential rupture. Unfortunately for human civilization, Mandel—a veteran of dystopian fiction—has previously proved herself an unwitting forecaster of very real geopolitical crises. Her 2014 novel Station Eleven was set in the wake of a global pandemic. Readers flocked to it six years later, and an HBO adaptation was quick to follow. Mandel—who, I should note, is Canadian—begins Exit Party in Los Angeles in 2031, when a curfew and foreign military occupation of the city are lifted after a U.S. civil war. “The United States had come undone following a coup d’état. Several states had seceded within a week of the coup, either alone or in alliances with neighbors,” she writes. The Republic of California is now its own country, one of “multiple small nations and city-states with ever-shifting borders and countless combatants, militants battling for control across the former nation.” To mark the first curfew-free night, protagonist Ari Waker and her friends attend a party. Mandel describes the fete in painstaking detail. Only later in the story does it become clear to readers that this technical play-by-play has a function: The party—and the bizarre, inexplicable events that occur there—are the foundation for a sci-fi journey through two parallel trajectories for the former United States. Understanding what occurred at the party is essential to understanding all that follows. Although the Republic of California is comparatively stable (“and therefore unaffordable,” Mandel writes—some things never change), most of the rest of the former United States is in shambles. Abandoned Staples office supply stores have become camps for internally displaced people, whose children attend makeshift schools housed at TGI Fridays; militias set up their headquarters in erstwhile shopping malls. (Washington, D.C., locals may be interested to learn that one of the most powerful armed groups is based in Silver Spring, Maryland.) To make ends meet, Ari finds herself drawn into a criminal web dealing weapons to rival militias—a journey that eventually leads her to flee to Paris. But while European borders seem mostly intact, the continent has its own problems. “In those days France was dangerous because everywhere was dangerous,” Mandel writes. Countries seek to gird against the effects of climate change by building Simpsons-esque domes over wealthy areas, creating new classes of haves and have-nots. It is in France that Ari, through links to that party in Los Angeles—and a dose of quantum physics—discovers an alternate path for the former United States. In the totalitarian United State, surveillance ensures prosperity. Futuristic bullet trains crisscross the country, and the entire population is immunized against cancer. But democracy is a thing of the past. Secret police not dissimilar to the East German Stasi make sure that “people who broke the rules disappeared.” Each of Mandel’s make-believe futures for the United States is equally unsettling. As Ari and fellow party guests toggle between scenarios of havoc and order, clashing with and sometimes abetting authority, it becomes clear that both systems have drawbacks. “There was a world where my homeland had fractured into disarray, and another where my homeland had closed like a fist,” Ari observes. What the two versions of the United States have in common, however, is that residents are tired—of tyranny, tumult, and struggling to get by. In believing that it’s “an exhausting moment to be alive,” they are no different from their real-life compatriots in 2026. As Ari narrates: “We were Americans, which is another way of saying that chaos felt like home.”—Allison Meakem The Floating World: A Novel Ben Eastham (Astra House, 288 pp., $26, September 2026) If there is anyone well positioned to write satisfying fiction about contemporary art, it’s Ben Eastham. The co-founder of the White Review and a regular critic for the Guardian, Eastham has made a name for himself by variously decoding the art world’s relationship to its bedfellows of power and capital, and dissecting—with compassion—works of art in ways that render them accessible, anew, or otherwise worthy of attention. So it is little surprise that Eastham’s debut novel, The Floating World, is at once a humorous send-up of this rarefied but often-mocked industry and a moving meditation on morality, grief, and the miracles that art may yet offer. The premise of Eastham’s novel slots neatly into the ultrarich-on-an-island genre popularized in recent years by films such as Glass Onion and The Menu, though it perhaps owes more to The Magus, John Fowles’ 1965 masterpiece about a young Englishman enthralled by an enigmatic Greek art collector. Like Nicholas Urfe, the disillusioned yet romantic protagonist of that novel, Eastham’s unnamed narrator is a writer who arrives on a remote island in the Aegean to find himself swept up in schemes beyond his grasp, soon unable to decipher reality from artifice. This recently widowed narrator has left London for Greece to work on an immersive exhibition by a renowned artist that will inaugurate the so-called Floating World, an island community ensconced in a giant dome. A settlement was originally constructed on the island in the 1950s as a utopian community for mine workers and their families after the discovery of rare-earth deposits, only to be abandoned during an economic downturn two decades later. Now, a billionaire heir to an arms manufacturing corporation has set his sights on resurrecting the site as a climate haven. The project is described, by various characters, as a “tax haven,” the heir’s “ideal city-state,” a “doomsday bunker for billionaires,” and “a sustainable, holistic, homeostatic community for powerful people who want insurance against the end of the world.” The narrator is aware that his work amounts to propaganda for an ethically dubious project but is eager for a distraction from his grief. And while he is often critical of the art world and its excesses, he is also attuned to art’s capacity to console and delight, especially amid the great crises of our time, from inequality to humanitarian suffering to ecological catastrophe. (Incidentally, the narrator’s emotional state appears to correlate to his charitability—or lack thereof—toward the individuals and artwork he encounters. “I could overhear an artist telling the minister for National Heritage that his work resisted categorization, even though I knew his work to be categorically shit,” he recounts at one particularly low point.) Contemporary art may be the cultural expression of runaway capitalism and globalization, the narrator thinks, but hasn’t art always been entangled with economic realities, whether that took the form of Renaissance masters exalting Italian merchants or the abstract expressionists propping up the U.S. vision of free-market liberalism? The art world, like much of society, may be fallen, but that hardly makes it irredeemable. At one point, the narrator reflects on a postcard of a painting based on an Albrecht Dürer engraving: “This cheap reproduction of a picture that is preserved in a palace built on state power and spiritual corruption, painted five hundred years ago by an unremembered copyist from a copperplate engraving, is itself a miracle. It moves me in a way that I cannot rationalize away by its formal qualities … It exceeds the infrastructures by which we strive to make sense of it.”—Chloe Hadavas September Releases, in Brief Booker Prize-winning Jamaican author Marlon James returns with The Disappearers, a 640-page queer epic centered on 1980s Kingston. In Doireann Ni Ghriofa’s genre-defying Said the Dead, the archives of a storied asylum in Cork, Ireland, are brought to life. Autofiction meets sci-fi in video-game designer and novelist Naomi Alderman’s The Strangers. In the 12 stories collected in The Queen of Bad Influences, Jim Shephard finds humanity across catastrophes from 16th century Madrid to the seas of World War I. Min Jin Lee, of Pachinko fame, chronicles the impact of the 1997 Asian financial crisis on one Korean family in American Hagwon. With the fictional memoir Agrippa, historical fiction stalwart Robert Harris turns his eye toward the Emperor Augustus’ right-hand man. The long shadow of colonialism haunts a Brazilian family in Itamar Vieira Junior’s Saving the Fire, translated from the Portuguese by Johnny Lorenz. In Chloe Benjamin’s Under Story, a portal found at a scientific research base in Antarctica opens to a parallel universe. Vikas Swarup, the Indian diplomat whose debut novel inspired Slumdog Millionaire, offers up another high-stakes thriller, The Girl With Seven Lives. And Canadian playwright and novelist Jordan Tannahill’s The Living Realm doubles as a ghost story and a paean to queer Berlin.—CH Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Milei Renews Argentina’s Falklands Push
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.03
Milei Renews Argentina’s Falklands Push Buenos Aires is taking advantage of fraying ties between the United States and Britain. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Argentine President Javier Milei’s renewed push for the Falkland Islands, clashes between the Houthis and government forces in Yemen, and international airlines halting flights to Russia. World Brief will be off on Monday, Sept. 7, for the U.S. holiday of Labor Day. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Argentine President Javier Milei’s renewed push for the Falkland Islands, clashes between the Houthis and government forces in Yemen, and international airlines halting flights to Russia. World Brief will be off on Monday, Sept. 7, for the U.S. holiday of Labor Day. Falklands at the Forefront In a nationally televised address on Thursday, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to sanction companies drilling for oil near the Falkland Islands, a British-controlled territory that is also claimed by Argentina. Milei also announced new funding for a naval base in the country’s southernmost province, which would increase Buenos Aires’s military presence near the islands. “Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security,” Milei said, using the Argentine term for the archipelago. The sanctions threat is aimed at halting development on the Sea Lion project, a deep-sea oil field operated by the U.K.’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum. The companies intend to start drilling in the next few months and begin pumping oil in 2028. Rockhopper said in a statement that it doesn’t expect Milei’s announcement to have a “material effect” on those plans. U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, meanwhile, affirmed Britain’s “absolute and unshakeable” commitment to the Falklands on social media. “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” he said, referring to a 2013 referendum in which the islands’ residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining in the United Kingdom. Britain has ruled the islands almost continuously since 1833. In 1982, the Falklands War erupted when Argentina seized the islands. The British military retook the territory after 74 days, but the dispute over the islands’ sovereignty remains contentious. When Argentina and England met on the soccer pitch during the World Cup this summer, Argentina’s players celebrated their victory by holding a banner reading “Las Malvinas Son Argentinas” (“The Falklands Are Argentine”). When he took office in 2023, Milei appeared to de-emphasize the Falklands to prioritize a closer relationship with the United States, which has long maintained neutrality on the issue. However, he has increasingly expressed the traditional Argentine position in recent months in what some analysts see as an effort to counter falling domestic ratings. “Milei’s belated embrace of the Falklands demonstrates why Argentina’s claim to the islands will only grow more insistent going forward: Domestic politicians almost universally use the Falklands to prove their nationalist credentials,” Antonio De Loera-Brust wrote in Foreign Policy in July. Milei’s move to reignite the Falklands issue was also likely influenced by Britain’s fraying ties with the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump hinted earlier on Thursday that he may not support Britain in a conflict over the islands because of the country’s lack of support for the U.S. war against Iran. During his speech, Milei praised Trump and stressed the leaders’ close relationship. “Claiming British territory is no longer the obstacle that it once was for Argentina’s ties with Europe and the United States, which means that Argentine leaders no longer have to choose between issues,” writes De Loera-Brust. Today’s Most Read - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Ukraine’s Mood Swing by Adrian Karatnycky What We’re Following Escalating violence. At least 81 people were killed and thousands displaced in Yemen after the Iran-backed Houthis launched a ground assault on Thursday toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key chokepoint for international shipping at the southern end of the Red Sea. The attack is part of a Houthi effort to sever the government-controlled city of Taiz from the coast, capture the port city of Mokha, and ultimately control all traffic through the strait. Since declaring a blockade on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in July, the Houthis have continued to attack Saudi ships and facilities, raising concerns that a full-blown war with Riyadh could reignite. That would add an additional squeeze on global shipping and energy prices. U.S. diesel prices on Friday hit an all-time high at $5.85 a gallon. Experts say fuel prices are likely to stay high until shipping fully resumes in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance insisted on Thursday that the Trump administration is doing “a lot of things” to pressure Iran to stop shooting at commercial ships in the strait, and on Friday, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions against a minor Turkish investment bank and two subsidiaries that do business with Tehran. “While we hope no more banks will need to be sanctioned, that ultimately depends on how quickly the international community comes to its senses and ceases support of the murderous Iranian regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Yet repeated U.S. military strikes, an oil blockade, and crushing economic sanctions have so far failed to convince Iran’s leadership to back down. Treacherous skies. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that international airlines are beginning to heed his call to suspend flights to Russia. This follows his announcement earlier this week that Ukraine would be expanding drone attacks near Russian airports in an effort to disrupt Moscow’s economy. Ninety-seven flights to Russia were canceled on Thursday, according to data from FlightRadar24, including services operated by Turkish, Emirati, Egyptian, Armenian, Kuwaiti, and Tajik airlines. Air Tanzania announced that flights to Moscow would be suspended until Monday. “[W]e are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said in a Tuesday post on X. Ukraine has intensified its air campaign against Russia in recent months, with a new peak of around 16,000 drones crossing into Russian airspace in August. According to Russia’s Defense Ministry, its forces downed 416 Ukrainian drones between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. Fraught forum. The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), a six-day gathering of officials from 18 countries and territories, came to a close on Friday. The region has emerged as a primary strategic arena in the past decade amid a battle for influence between global powers such as China and the United States. The meetings, which were held in Palau this year—one of only 11 countries worldwide that recognize Taiwan—were marred by geopolitical tensions. Addressing China’s ballistic missile test-launch in the South Pacific in July was at the top of the agenda. But although the forum members agreed on Thursday to register their collective “concern” about the launch, the statement was far from a harsh rebuke, and even then it wasn’t unanimous: Nauru, an island nation that severed its diplomatic ties with Taiwan in 2024, dissented. Nevertheless, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told reporters that he thought the assembly had “got to a very good place,” and that even though Nauru “dissociated itself” from the joint statement, “that shouldn’t be a reason for why we shouldn’t be able to express a PIF position or a consensus position.” Last-minute withdrawals of top leaders from five member nations—Kiribati, Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa, and the Solomon Islands—overshadowed proceedings from the get-go and prompted suggestions that Chinese influence, stemming from its displeasure over the host location, could be to blame. New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters refrained from directly accusing Beijing of interfering, but he said that the collective absence was “highly suspicious.” What in the World? Provisional results on Tuesday showed that voters had approved a referendum on a new constitution in Guinea-Bissau. The new charter would expand presidential authority. Which of the below is not one of the powers it would grant to the president? A. Appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet B. Create and abolish ministries C. Unilaterally determine the military’s annual budget D. Dissolve parliament in a political crisis Odds and Ends It may be that “good things come to those who wait,” especially when it comes to the famously long Guinness pour, which takes 119.5 seconds to complete. But thieves wasted no time pulling off a heist of two truckloads of the stout beer this week from a depot near Liverpool in the United Kingdom. British police are now trying to recover the 70,000 pints, worth $155,000. Here’s hoping the thieves don’t plan to drink it all themselves. And the Answer Is… A. Unilaterally determine the military’s annual budget Coup leaders across Africa have changed strategies to retain power, sometimes extending transitional government windows, delaying elections, or using elections to legitimize their continued grip on power, Salah Ben Hammou and Sydney Dobbins wrote in July 2025. To take the rest of FP’s weekly international news quiz, click here, or sign up to be alerted when a new one is published. Maxine Davey is an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy.
