item.title: A N.Y. hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 4.74
A N.Y. hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back TROY, N.Y. — Like many residents of this aging industrial city on the Hudson River, Starletta Washington was stunned when she heard Troy's last remaining hospital planned to close its birthing center. "It was devastating," said Washington, who heads the local YWCA. Washington was born at the hospital and had her children there. She couldn't believe families would now have to get to a hospital half an hour away or face the prospect of an emergency delivery. "Nobody else was going to be born in the city of Troy unless they were born on a city bus, in the back of a cab, or, disgustingly, on the side of the street?" Washington said. "Blew my mind." Troy wasn't the first community to face this prospect. Since 2010, hospitals have closed hundreds of maternity units as cities and towns shrink and hospitals consolidate into larger systems. Troy found a more hopeful ending. Elected officials from both major parties joined patient advocates, mothers, midwives, doulas and community leaders like Washington to challenge Trinity Health, the large Catholic health system that owns Troy's hospital and birthing center. The campaign even united Planned Parenthood and the Catholic diocese. "Whether you were Republican or Democrat, or if you didn't vote, it literally brought everyone together," said Carmella Mantello, the city's Republican mayor. "Everyone just said, 'We can't let this happen.'" Throughout the country, healthcare remains a flash point as politicians square off ahead of November's elections. But in many places, Americans are also quietly finding common ground. In this small city, citizens were brought together by frustration over large, corporate health systems that can seem to put profits over patients. And they resolved to work together to keep critical medical services in their community. A community institution Babies have been delivered at Samaritan Hospital on a hill above Troy since this city's once bustling factories produced most of America's shirt collars a century ago. More recently, Samaritan's Burdett Birth Center had become a model for patient-focused care. Midwives and doulas work alongside OB-GYNs and support mothers who want to avoid a delivery by cesarean section unless necessary. Patient safety advocates have pushed for years to reduce surgical deliveries, which can lead to complications. At Burdett, only about a quarter of newborns are delivered by C-section, compared with about a third statewide, according to 2025 hospital data. Burdett also had fewer preterm births and fewer babies with low birth weights. "I wouldn't go anywhere else," said Lidia Zambrano-Madera, who gave birth to both her children at Burdett with the help of a midwife. For Zambrano-Madera, who recently opened a children's play center in Troy, Burdett offered another advantage: It was just five minutes from home. But three years ago, Trinity Health, a multibillion-dollar Michigan-based hospital system, said the birth center was losing money and would close. Families from Troy and surrounding Rensselaer County would have to deliver at another Trinity hospital in Albany, up to a half-hour's drive away. The hospitals are branded under St. Peter's Health Partners in the Albany region. "We've been frantic about trying not to cut the care at the bedside," said Steven Hanks, a physician who oversees Trinity hospitals in New York and New England. "But, you know, you get to a point where you can only consolidate so much. You can only spread people so thin, and then you have to start taking harder looks at your actual services." Corporate backlash Trinity's plans — news of which broke in a local newspaper — came without warning, surprising the obstetrical staff and community leaders. They set off a firestorm. Within days, midwives, mothers, community leaders and politicians held a rally at the YWCA in downtown Troy. Others would follow. Volunteers led by doulas and midwives made T-shirts and handed out pink "Save Burdett" signs at the local farmers market. Activists were outraged that the hospital hadn't adequately assessed the impact of the closure, particularly on low-income families. They conducted a community survey that found 1 in 4 Troy residents didn't have access to a car and would have trouble getting to Albany. The campaign drew on deep connections that many residents had to Burdett. "They realized what a gem Burdett is, and what a great community service they provide," said Jessica Hayek, a doula and birth educator who helped lead the campaign. Hayek and others also tapped into deep-seated frustration with Trinity, a healthcare behemoth that operates 91 hospitals and last year recorded more than $25 billion in revenue and a healthy operating margin that topped 5%. "Trinity Health is in the Midwest, and they are not in the community," Hayek said. "So when you're looking at just the numbers from an office in the Midwest somewhere, they're not looking at the benefit that this place has on the community." Hayek describes herself as a liberal Democrat. But Trinity's focus on its bottom line also irked many Republicans, including Mantello, who was the City Council president at the time. "The whole hospital scene has changed," Mantello said. "It was very personable. You had nurses and doctors who were able to give more care and spend more time with patients." Now, by contrast, many hospitals have what she described as a "more corporate type of atmosphere." Even the Catholic bishop decried the planned closure of the birthing center as out of step with the values of his faith and the hospital system's. "Nothing is more central to the Catholic healthcare mission than supporting life and all those who bring it into the world," Bishop Edward Scharfenberger said after Trinity announced the closure plan. Scharfenberger has since retired. A bipartisan solution Despite the backlash, Trinity Health executives for months insisted they had no choice. The system even sued the state to push through the closure. Ultimately, though, powerful state officials, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, joined the fight to save the birthing center, launching an investigation into the proposed closure and hosting a daylong hearing in Troy. State Assemblyman John T. McDonald III, a Democrat who represents Troy, worked with Republican elected officials, including the county executive and the state senator representing Troy, to secure $5 million in state funding to help keep Burdett open. "You had a Democrat and a bunch of Republicans all working together on the same issue," McDonald said, "because, at the end of the day, our job is to listen to what the public has to say." Nearly a year after announcing the closure, Trinity reversed itself and said Burdett would remain open. Lois Uttley, a New York City-based researcher and activist who has worked with communities facing hospital consolidation, said Troy's success reflects a growing bipartisan suspicion of big corporate healthcare organizations. "The executives of these health systems will tell the community that joining a big health system will be good, that the quality of care will improve, that efficiencies will mean they can keep the costs low," Uttley said. "But what I have seen over the last 30 years of work is that those promises often are broken." As hospitals close or downsize, she said, communities are catching on. "They're becoming more skeptical." There's another, more hopeful lesson in Troy's success, said McDonald, the state assemblyman. "If we take down our swords," he said, "and put out our arms, maybe we can get something done." KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

item.title: Why too many women are prescribed antibiotics for UTIs they don't have
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 4.35
Why too many women are prescribed antibiotics for UTIs they don't have Maria Uloko sees the same scenario in her urology practice in Los Angeles every day: A woman has been diagnosed with recurrent urinary tract infections (which means she's had at least two in six months or three in a year), taken repeated rounds of antibiotics, and feels confused as to why the infections keep coming back. Then, Uloko tells these patients something that often feels both revelatory and frustrating. "Most of them don't actually have UTIs, even though that's been their diagnosis time and time again," she says. "In fact, millions of women are being treated for UTIs they may not actually have." Uloko is the co-author of a recent study published in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that backs this up. She and her fellow researchers reviewed the medical records of 253 women with recurrent UTIs and found that just 15% showed evidence of problems that were limited to the bladder or urinary tract. The remaining 85% had signs of hormonally driven inflammation of the vulvar region and 75% had pelvic floor dysfunction. These conditions produce identical symptoms as UTIs — burning with urination, urgency, frequency, and/or lower abdominal pain — but require different treatment. "What we found is that in women with recurrent UTIs, the majority didn't have a bladder problem at all; they had a vulvar problem," says Uloko. Uloko's study provides insights that could help patients with urinary tract symptoms, says Melissa Kaufman, professor and chief of the division of reconstructive urology and pelvic health at Vanderbilt University Medical Center who was not involved in the research. "These findings will accelerate our discipline's investigations into a comprehensive unifying hypothesis to more precisely optimize care," she said via email. Why are these vulvar conditions getting missed? One reason is the current diagnostic process for UTIs. When a patient comes in with classic UTI symptoms, the first thing most clinicians order is a screening test called a urinalysis, which detects the presence of inflammation — not bacteria. To determine whether there's a bacterial infection, that urine must be cultured. What's more, that urine sample must be a "clean catch," which requires thoroughly cleaning the urinary tract opening and surrounding areas and collecting only the midstream of urine, something not all patients are instructed on how to do, says Kaufman. "But because patients are suffering in real time, clinicians often start them on a broad-spectrum antibiotic right away if that urinalysis comes back positive and adjust the medication if needed once the culture comes back," says Uloko. There's also a lack of training among medical professionals, says Uloko, adding that doctors are taught that when a patient presents with classic UTI symptoms, it should be considered a UTI until proven otherwise. "We do the urinalysis, send the culture, start the antibiotic, and for the patients who get better, amazing," she says. For the patients who don't get better, the cycle continues "because the doctor, who hasn't been taught how the vulva relates to urinary, colon, and sexual health, doesn't know what else to do." Overlooked causes of UTI-like symptoms The truth is that lower urinary tract symptoms that may look and feel like a UTI can be caused by things other than bacteria, says Lindsey Burnett, a urogynecologist, assistant professor at the University of California, San Diego, and co-author with Uloko on the study. For example, a loss of hormones to the vulvar tissue can cause inflammation, a condition called hormonally mediated vestibulodynia. This can happen due to natural physiological changes to hormones that happen during breastfeeding and menopause. It can also happen if you're taking medications that impact hormones. For example, oral birth control is one of the most commonly prescribed anti-androgen medications that can disrupt the hormonal balance in the vulvar tissue and cause inflammation that prompts UTI-like symptoms. Other commonly prescribed medications that can cause vulvar inflammation include medications for acne (such as isotretinoin, sold as Accutane) and hair loss (such as minoxidil, sold as Rogaine); oncologic treatments for breast, ovarian, and/or uterine cancer (such as aromatase inhibitors and selective estrogen receptor modulators); and hormone therapies for endometriosis or fibroids. The genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM, a collection of symptoms caused by the decline in estrogen and other sex hormones during menopause, can also affect the tissues of the vagina, vulva, bladder, and urethra and cause UTI-like symptoms. Chronic inflammation due to GSM can also prompt the pelvic floor muscles to go into a state of reactive guarding, says Uloko, which can make them hypertonic (too tight) and can further disrupt bladder function. Things get even more complex when you consider that these hormonal changes can also alter the balance of good and bad bacteria in the urinary tract and vagina. When levels of hormones like estrogen and testosterone are disrupted, the good bacteria decline, which puts patients at risk for developing bacterial UTIs, says Uloko. "So now you have a patient who is testing positive on urinalysis, sometimes growing actual bacteria on culture, receiving antibiotics, getting temporary relief mostly because of the anti-inflammatory properties in antibiotics, and then cycling right back into symptoms because the underlying hormonal and vulvar dysfunction was never addressed." What to ask your doctor to make sure you're getting the best care If you suspect your recurrent UTIs may be caused by a vulvar issue that has yet to be diagnosed, ask your clinician a few key questions: Was my urine culture positive for bacteria? Remember, the first test typically given to patients who present with UTI-like symptoms is a urinalysis, which tests for inflammation — not a bacterial infection. Could my symptoms be due to hormone changes affecting my vulva due to medications I'm taking, or the menopause transition? There are many conditions that have overlapping symptoms with lower urinary tract symptoms, but getting an appropriate diagnosis for the condition causing your symptoms "requires that someone have the wherewithal and the care to screen and diagnose appropriately in women," says Kaufman. This can be surprisingly difficult to find. The antidote is to arm yourself with knowledge and name it at your next appointment. You might say to your clinician, "I read that taking the birth control pill could impact my hormones in such a way that it causes vulvovaginal symptoms that could mimic common UTI symptoms. Can we talk about this being a potential factor in my case?" Uloko recommends that patients print the research and bring it to their appointment. "If you've asked directly and collaboratively, 'Have you considered this angle for my recurrent UTIs?' and you're dismissed, ask the clinician to document the refusal in your chart, in writing," she says. "This changes behavior and leaves you a record." Have my vulvar tissue and pelvic floor been examined? Vulvovaginal health and pelvic health are just as important as bladder function and should be evaluated, says Burnett. "I can't tell you how many patients I see who have spasms of their pelvic floor muscles, and that's probably what's causing their urinary symptoms." Unfortunately, many clinicians aren't comfortable doing even a basic physical exam of a woman's pelvis, says Kaufman. "It's a simple exam to look for diagnostic changes around the vulva and openings to the vagina and urethra — one that doesn't even have to involve a speculum or a pap smear," she says. "And it's too often a barrier to treatment for many of these conditions with symptoms that mimic a UTI." If you don't think your primary care doctor is doing an adequate physical exam or answering your questions, make an appointment with a specialist. Start with a urologist, who has specialized training in treating UTIs and understands that the bladder is part of an interconnected genitourinary system. Other good options include a urogynecologist, gynecologist, or Menopause Society-certified practitioner. Am I a candidate for vaginal estrogen or DHEA? The American Urological Association has published guidelines for multiple conditions that can all present with UTI-like symptoms — overactive bladder, recurrent UTIs, and GSM — and they clearly state that low-dose vaginal estrogen or DHEA is an effective treatment. "There are a number of randomized control trials and systematic reviews that demonstrate that low-dose vaginal estrogen reduces the risk for recurrent urinary tract infections in perimenopausal and post-menopausal women," says Kaufman, one of the authors of the association's guidelines. You can even bring these guidelines with you to your next healthcare visit to jumpstart the conversation with your clinician. "As urologists, we do a pretty good job of the urinary part of the evaluation — the bladder, ureters, and kidneys," says Uloko. "Where we fall short is the genital part, and that requires a much broader understanding of the pelvic ecosystem as a whole — the hormonal environment, vulvar tissue, and pelvic floor musculature, all influencing each other and all capable of producing symptoms that look exactly like a UTI." Meghan Rabbitt is a journalist and author of The New Rules of Women's Health.

item.title: From bottles to bakery: How scientists create edible cookies from recycled plastic
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 3.77
From bottles to bakery: How scientists create edible cookies from recycled plastic New research at the American Chemical Society meeting showcased a potentially edible cookie made out of — plastic! SCOTT SIMON, HOST: Plastic pollution is a major problem 'round the globe. What if we could recycle some of that plastic by eating it? NPR science reporter Ari Daniel tells us about researchers who use plastic to make cookies. Didn't get to taste them, though. ARI DANIEL, BYLINE: Transforming plastic into a snack may sound a little tough to swallow. But Lahiru Jayakody, a synthetic microbiologist at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, says, just think of a cow. LAHIRU JAYAKODY: Can you eat grass? No. But cow take the grass, and it produce milk. We use milk to make many, many different product. DANIEL: In other words, living creatures are like chemistry labs, converting raw ingredients into new materials. Microbes excel at this kind of thing, so Jayakody decided to try genetically engineering yeast to digest plastic - specifically the kind often used in water bottles and food packaging. Ph.D. student Sandhya Jayasekara first took the intact plastic, along with ground-up corn husks and stalks, and broke it all down into simpler molecules. SANDHYA JAYASEKARA: So those molecules are available as a food for the yeast. DANIEL: She then gave it to the yeast, which processed this mix of disintegrated plastic and corn to make a gluey protein paste, which Jayasekara mixed with vanilla and beta-carotene that were produced by other yeast and different food ingredients, like oatmeal. A 3D food printer then turned that slurry into small cookies. Here's Lahiru Jayakody. JAYAKODY: There is no micro- or nanoplastic embedded into this cookie. So we are not eating plastic. DANIEL: Nor has anyone actually eaten the cookie yet. There are still safety tests to be done. The process is pricey, uses a lot of energy, and not much of the plastic makes it into the final cookie. JAYAKODY: This is a proof of concept, right? JAYASEKARA: Kind of a beginning of a journey. DANIEL: Still, the researchers say they hope the cookies may, at some point, be made from plastic waste on-site in extreme or difficult environments, like outer space or disaster zones. This work was presented at the American Chemical Society meeting in Chicago last week. PAMELA SILVER: I think the concept is right on the mark. DANIEL: Pamela Silver is a synthetic biologist at Harvard Medical School who wasn't involved in the research. She says the idea of turning plastic into food isn't new. The real barriers to making it a reality tend to be scalability, cost and texture. SILVER: Texture comes from fats. So in all the foods you eat - meat, cheese, everything you eat - it's the fat that makes you enjoy it. DANIEL: There's not much fat in these new plastic-derived cookies. But Silver welcomes this kind of thinking, which may one day provide a sweeter solution to a less-than-palatable problem. Ari Daniel, NPR News. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. item.title: Exclusive: Meet the inaugural winner of Fat Marmot Week
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 3.29
Exclusive: Meet the inaugural winner of Fat Marmot Week Annnnd there's a winner in the first-ever Fat Marmot Week! The competition was among eight yellow-bellied marmots in Colorado vying to gain the most weight before winter hibernation. The Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory's Marmot Project hosted Fat Marmot Week as a way to hype up these cat-sized alpine rodents, in the face of cuts to research funding. Yellow-bellied marmots hibernate to survive the snowy high-mountain winters. They curl up, lower their body temperatures, and slow their breathing. They spend more than half the year like this, relying on their stored fat. Thus: Fat Marmot Week. Marmot enthusiasts were encouraged to cheer on Dawn, G, Dan's Hat, Citroen, Open Kite, 1, Dandelion, and Stonehenge as they spent the month of August bulking up. Weekend Edition had the honor of exclusively announcing the popular vote winner — the marmot that the public crowned as the fattest of them all. Congratulations to Dawn! Your chunky champion is a father who the RMBL says "enjoys the taste of rocks." The Marmot Project also announced that Dawn was the competition's "true" winner on Saturday, based on researchers' estimation of the animals' actual size. Clocking in with a 4.5lb weight gain for a total of 13lbs, congratulations to Dawn for gaining the most weight! Weekend Edition staff also held an informal vote, picking Stonehenge, a resilient mother who lost her litter to a hungry badger earlier this year. The competition was inspired by Alaska's Fat Bear Week — when more than a million people cast votes for the chonkiest brown bear. Fun fact: Marmots are the biggest true hibernators in the world. Bears do not hibernate, they go into a sort of deep sleep called "torpor." The Marmot Project has been researching these rodents since 1962. It's one of the longest-running projects studying individually tagged mammals in the wild. "These long-term studies provide us the insights to understand how organisms, plants, animals, whatever, respond to a changing environment," said Dan Blumstein, a professor at UCLA who runs the Marmot Project, in an interview with NPR's Ayesha Rascoe earlier this month. Fat Marmot Week is not the only way that the project is creatively working to restore lost funds. Blumstein opened an OnlyFans account, OnlyMarms, promising "uncensored marmot content" to subscribers. At the beginning of August, OnlyMarms had generated about $4,000 for research funding. Blumstein hopes the hoopla around Fat Marmot Week will boost donations. "We have some funding for next year, but after that, it's looking very dire," Blumstein said.

item.title: Meta's multi-billion settlement launches the next phase of national tech regulation
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Score: 3.81
Meta's multi-billion settlement launches the next phase of national tech regulation Meta's settlement with states in a child safety case this week had a big payout, but the attorneys general have their eyes on a bigger prize: national regulation of social media companies. SCOTT SIMON, HOST: When Meta agreed to settle a landmark child safety case this week, it said it would pay up to $17 billion in penalties. That's among the largest settlement payouts by any company in U.S. history. But that's not what the state attorneys general who brought the case were excited about. Here's California's AG Rob Bonta. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) ROB BONTA: It's not about the money, although the money is important and significant. The lead here is the injunctive relief. SIMON: By injunctive relief, he means changes Meta has to make to its platforms so they're considered safer for teens, changes the company has resisted and that Congress hasn't been able to achieve through legislation. NPR tech correspondent John Ruwitch joins us now. John, thanks for being with us. JOHN RUWITCH, BYLINE: Sure thing, Scott. SIMON: Before we get into this legal strategy, what kind of changes did Meta agree to? RUWITCH: Sure. So this case was a reaction to widespread concern that social media can be unhealthy for kids and has fueled a teen mental health crisis in America. The states argued in their case that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to be addictive to kids. It knew they were getting exposed to dangerous content and lied about it to the public. So in the settlement, Meta agreed to make changes to its platforms that aim to better protect kids from addiction. That includes time limits on daily use, blockers at night and during the school day, no access to beauty filters, no information for minors about how many people like their posts. The idea is that teens would be on these platforms less. SIMON: Why is this the focus for these state AGs rather than the money? RUWITCH: Yeah. Look, the money is going to be used to fund things like mental health programs and after-school activities. That's all meaningful. But the AGs are trying to do something that's much bigger. Part of this settlement is an effort to get three other big social media platforms - Meta's main competitors - to sign on to similar use restrictions for kids. Those platforms are YouTube, TikTok and Snap. They were not involved in this specific trial, but they've been named in all kinds of other lawsuits that are related to kids and mental health. We reached out to these companies for comment but haven't heard back. For Meta, having them agree eventually to the same rules would level the competitive playing field and make sure that its users don't just migrate to other platforms with looser rules. For the AGs, it's part of a pretty interesting gambit. SIMON: What is the gambit? RUWITCH: Yeah. The AGs aren't just enforcing the law here. They're trying to create a regulatory regime around social media companies where there isn't one right now. I asked William Tong about this. He's the AG for Connecticut, which was part of the case, and I wanted to know why the state attorneys general are being so aggressive in pushing these changes to how social media companies operate. WILLIAM TONG: It's in large part because there are large areas of American life that require action or require protective action to keep people safe where Congress has not been effective. RUWITCH: Basically, they're using litigation to replace legislation. Now, to be fair, some states have put in place regulations, but at a national level, most attempts have failed. Timothy Lytton, a law professor at Georgia State University, says that is in part because Big Tech is rich and powerful and has been very successful in lobbying against regulation. TIMOTHY LYTTON: And so that's why you see, I think, attorneys general stepping in where legislatures and governors have not been willing to go. RUWITCH: He says they're acting as a kind of insulated counterbalance to the politics of it all. And it's worth noting, the AGs in this case were a bipartisan group. SIMON: That is interesting in these times. How do you rate their chance of success in reining in these social media companies? RUWITCH: Well, a lot has to fall in place for that to happen. We don't know yet, for instance, when or how these other companies are going to fall in line or if they will. Experts say the attorneys general are signaling - in this case and others - that they don't want to destroy these social media companies with crushing penalties but instead want to work with them. But this settlement contains an implicit threat. Here's Timothy Lytton again. LYTTON: Everybody in this particular industry is now on notice that if you don't exercise the kind of restraint that Meta is now starting to agree to, that you can probably expect to see some sort of legal action. RUWITCH: He says the case raises public pressure on legislators to move on the issue. People are really mad about this. But he says meaningful regulation in America actually often comes through litigation like this. It's a feature of our system, not a bug. SIMON: NPR's John Ruwitch. Thanks so much. RUWITCH: You're welcome. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. item.title: U.S. strikes three Iranian oil tankers in renewal of hostilities
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 4.16
U.S. strikes three Iranian oil tankers in renewal of hostilities The U.S. strikes three Iranian oil tankers after Iran targets two American warships, in the latest exchange over shipping and the Strait of Hormuz. JOEL ROSE, HOST: The confrontation between the United States and Iran has flared up again this weekend with tit-for-tat strikes that are becoming a pattern in this conflict. The U.S. says it struck three Iranian oil tankers after Iran launched missiles at two American warships, putting fresh pressure on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and on global oil prices. The latest exchange comes after a weekslong lull in U.S.-Iran military action. NPR's international correspondent Carrie Kahn is in the region. So tell us what happened today. CARRIE KAHN, BYLINE: The U.S. military says Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or the IRGC, launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S. naval vessels. It was an aircraft carrier and a guided missile destroyer. CENTCOM says both ships were able to evade those attacks, and in retaliation, the U.S. struck three Iranian oil tankers, destroying all of them. One was near Iran's key Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. That's the heart of Iran's oil export system. Another of the three was actually in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM says it was hit several times, and its crew was forced to abandon ship. In its statement, CENTCOM said, the tanker is part of a, quote, "multibillion-dollar shadow network that's used to fund Iran's Revolutionary Guard. CENTCOM's commander said, quote, "if you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost taking out three of yours." ROSE: It's now been more than six months since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, but it had been relatively quiet for many weeks now. Why have the strikes picked up this weekend? KAHN: The U.S. says it's dealing with attacks and threats to commercial shipping, and it began the resumption of strikes last weekend and into the week hitting several sites in Iran. One of those was a U.S. strike on a wedding celebration that killed at least five people and injured dozens. That's according to Iran. Washington said it is investigating those claims. Iran immediately retaliated, launching drones and missiles at U.S. targets, military bases in the Gulf. Iran's foreign ministry condemned today's U.S. strikes, calling the actions illegal and a clear threat to international peace and the security of commercial shipping. And on state media today, Iran threatened to increase and expand its strikes on U.S. military vessels if the U.S. kept blocking Iranian ports and targeting its ships. ROSE: So what does the resumption of strikes and retaliation mean for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz? Who actually controls it right now? KAHN: Well, Iran says it controls the strait, and it has actually been in negotiations with Oman to determine some new fees and passage restrictions. President Trump has said the U.S. is in control. It has the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and a large presence there attempting to keep commercial traffic moving. Do remember that before the war began in February, the strait was open to all commercial traffic, without any restrictions and the threats we're seeing now. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center says vessel traffic through the strait now is down again to around 90% from pre-war level while Brent Crude has risen above $90 a barrel again this week. President Trump characterized the war as, quote, "small potatoes.' He said that this week. And Vice President JD Vance declined to even describe the conflict as a war. But both know that whatever the terminology each side is using, the longer the cycle of this back-and-forth strikes drags on, the greater the disruption to energy markets and the more tangible the economic impact becomes both in the U.S. and, of course, globally. ROSE: That's NPR's Carrie Kahn in Tel Aviv. Thanks, Carrie. KAHN: You're welcome. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. item.title: 2 trapped workers rescued from a hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 3.27
Rescuers pull 2 trapped workers from a hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from an underground tunnel at a hydropower plant Friday, raising hopes of reaching dozens of others believed to be trapped nine days after deadly floods swept away villages and submerged the Himalayan region in mud and debris. Search teams first heard voices from inside the tunnel in the morning, allowing them to locate the two men, Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane said. Images showed a rescuer carrying one of the workers, covered in mud, on his back, while soldiers on either side helped. One of those rescued said more people are alive inside the tunnel, according to army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, and the search is ongoing. "I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of those rescued, told The Associated Press. Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue, and Neupane posted about the second on his Facebook page shortly after. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, and Maharjan said his family was on its way there. One of the survivors was in critical condition, according to a statement from the prime minister's office. Officials identified the men as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor. They were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A plant. About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in various tunnels, according to authorities. About 115 are believed trapped in the tunnel at Trishuli 3A alone, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal. Nepal's Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page that officials "are waiting for the rescue of more and more people." At least 1,287 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency. China said Friday 31 people were killed and 531 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, according to Chinese official news agency Xinhua. Nepal's disaster agency estimated Friday that flooding caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.

item.title: 10 U.S. cities where remote workers are buying homes in 2026 — ranked by value
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.19
10 U.S. cities where remote workers are buying homes in 2026 — ranked by value The best cities for remote workers to buy a home in 2026, ranked by value, combine affordable prices, strong job growth and, in some cases, thousands in relocation cash A record share of American house hunters are looking to leave their metro area, and the freedom to work from anywhere is a major reason why. Redfin found that 19.1% of house hunters searched for homes in a different part of the country in the first quarter of 2026. That is the highest share since the company began tracking migration in 2021. Roughly a quarter of paid U.S. workdays are still performed from home, according to Stanford University's Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes. That share has held steady since 2023, even as some employers have pushed for a return to the office. For millions of workers, that flexibility has become a financial strategy: trade a big-city paycheck for a small-city mortgage. Cities have noticed. Some are simply capitalizing on housing stock that never got expensive in the first place, backed by job growth in aerospace, health care, logistics or advanced manufacturing. Others have gone further, building cash-incentive programs that pay remote workers directly to relocate, and in several cases to buy a house once they arrive. Both strategies point to the same conclusion. The best deal for a remote worker in 2026 is rarely the city with the single lowest price tag. It is the city where a below-average mortgage payment meets an above-average shot at building equity, a stable job market and infrastructure that can support a full-time home office. This list ranks 10 U.S. cities using a broader definition of value. Three factors matter most: home prices relative to the national median, income and job growth that support future appreciation, and direct relocation incentives where they exist. In a few cities, those incentives alone can offset a down payment before a single moving box gets packed. Some entries are well-known relocation hubs. Others are quieter markets that have simply stayed affordable while their local economies expanded. Together, they show where a remote paycheck stretches the furthest in 2026, and why. Topeka, Kansas pays homebuyers up to $15,000 to relocate Credit: Nils Huenerfuerst / Unsplash Topeka offers the cheapest homes on this list, and one of the country's largest cash incentives for buying one. The Choose Topeka program, run by the Greater Topeka Partnership, pays up to $15,000 toward a home purchase for workers who take a job with a participating local employer. Remote employees can qualify too, typically for a smaller amount, after a three-month waiting period. The math starts from an already low base. Zillow's home value index put the typical Topeka home at $190,096 in March 2026. Redfin recorded a median sale price of $184,839 in May, up 8.7% from a year earlier. Both figures sit close to half the national median home value of roughly $372,000. A remote worker who qualifies for the incentive could cover a meaningful share of a standard down payment before making a first mortgage payment. Choose Topeka has run since 2019 and has drawn hundreds of applicants from dozens of states. The program works by pairing incoming workers with local employers in health care, insurance, state government and manufacturing, since Topeka is the Kansas state capital and home to a large public-sector workforce. That employer relationship also keeps the incentive funded: participating companies split the cost of each award with the Greater Topeka Partnership and its local development partners. Beyond the incentive, Topeka's appeal rests on cost of living broadly, not housing alone. Groceries, utilities and transportation all run below national averages across Kansas. The combined effect of a below-median mortgage and below-median monthly expenses is what gives Topeka the top spot on this list, ahead of cities with flashier job markets. The trade-off is scale. Topeka's metro population sits under 235,000, with fewer dining and entertainment options than a larger city and a slower pace that will not suit every remote worker leaving a coastal metro. For someone prioritizing a low mortgage payment and a straightforward relocation process over big-city amenities, Topeka is difficult to beat on pure value. Tulsa, Oklahoma still offers $10,000 in cash to remote workers Lucas Alexander / Unsplash Tulsa Remote pays $10,000 to remote workers who relocate to the city, with no requirement to buy a home. More than 4,000 people have joined since the program launched in 2018. About 80% remain in Tulsa beyond their initial one-year commitment, according to program figures reported by Forbes in August 2026. That retention rate matters for this list because it points to what happens after the check clears: many participants stay, and a meaningful share go on to buy. Tulsa makes that step easier than most cities its size. Redfin recorded a median sale price of $254,000 for the three months ending in June 2026, which the company puts at 34% below the national average. Zillow's home value index shows a similar typical value of $221,628. Overall cost of living in Tulsa runs 17% below the national average, according to Redfin. Participants also get access to a free three-year membership at 36 Degrees North, a large coworking space downtown, along with networking events built for remote and self-employed workers. That infrastructure matters in a city that is not a traditional tech hub. Tulsa's economy still leans on energy, aerospace and health care, which gives incoming remote workers a local job market to fall back on if a client or employer relationship ends. Oklahoma does levy a state income tax, unlike a few other entries on this list, so the state-tax savings some remote workers chase elsewhere do not apply here. What Tulsa offers instead is a mature, well-tested relocation program and a housing market that has stayed affordable even as national prices climbed. The city's Arts District and Route 66 corridor have also drawn steady investment, giving new arrivals a walkable core rather than just a low mortgage payment. For a remote worker weighing multiple cash-incentive cities, Tulsa's combination of program longevity, home prices well below the national median and a diversified local economy makes it one of the safer bets on this list. Morgantown, West Virginia adds a $12,000 grant to mountain-town prices Credit: Canva Images Ascend West Virginia pays remote workers $12,000 to move to one of six host communities, plus a free year of outdoor recreation gear and coworking access. Morgantown, home to West Virginia University, is the program's original and largest location. The program launched in April 2021 as Ascend Morgantown. It has since expanded to five more communities: Shepherdstown and the Eastern Panhandle, Lewisburg and the Greenbrier Valley, Greater Elkins, the New River Gorge, and, most recently, Charleston. Applicants must be full-time remote employees or self-employed business owners based outside West Virginia, and most of the $12,000 is paid out over the first 12 months after arrival. Morgantown's housing market backs up the pitch. Zillow's home value index put the typical home there at roughly $272,000 in early 2026, well below the national figure of about $372,000. Redfin and other trackers have shown a similar range, generally between $240,000 and $310,000 depending on the month and the mix of homes sold. A price-to-income analysis by the housing site Amortio put Morgantown's ratio of home price to median household income at 5.8, a level it classifies as affordable relative to many U.S. metros. West Virginia does charge a state income tax, ranging from 3% to 6.5% depending on income and filing status, so this is not a tax-free relocation. What it does offer is genuine outdoor access: whitewater rivers, climbing routes and mountain-biking trails sit minutes from downtown in several of the program's host communities, and Morgantown sits about an hour from Pittsburgh for anyone who wants occasional big-city amenities without living in one. The trade-off is job market depth. Outside of West Virginia University and a handful of health systems, local employment options are limited, which is precisely why Ascend WV targets people who do not need a local employer. For remote workers who fit that description, the combination of cash, low prices and mountain access is hard to match elsewhere on this list. Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania delivers big-city jobs at a fraction of the price Credit: Tyler Rutherford / Unsplash Pittsburgh offers some of the lowest home prices of any major U.S. metro, without the incentive programs some smaller cities need to compete. Zillow's home value index put the typical Pittsburgh home at roughly $243,000 in mid-2026. Redfin recorded a median sale price of $258,000 in a recent month, up 11.2% from a year earlier. Those figures sit roughly a third below the national median, according to several local real estate analyses that track both Pittsburgh and statewide Pennsylvania prices. That gap has held even as Pittsburgh's economy has shifted away from its industrial past. UPMC, the region's dominant health system, is the largest employer in Pennsylvania. Carnegie Mellon University has built a robotics and artificial intelligence research cluster that feeds a growing local tech sector, and the University of Pittsburgh adds another large base of research funding and jobs. Local unemployment sat at 3.8% in early 2026, below the national rate, with particular demand for software engineers, robotics researchers and health care professionals. For a remote worker relocating from a coastal tech hub, that combination matters. Low housing costs paired with an active knowledge-economy job market offer a backup option that pure cash-incentive towns cannot always match. If a remote job disappears, Pittsburgh still has employers hiring in adjacent fields. The city's older housing stock is part of the appeal. Walkable neighborhoods including Lawrenceville, Shadyside and Squirrel Hill combine renovated row houses with a scale that is hard to find in most growing Sun Belt metros. Winters are colder than anywhere else on this list, and heating costs run above the national average as a result, which is worth factoring into any monthly budget. Pennsylvania applies a flat state income tax of a little over 3%, so Pittsburgh will not deliver the tax-free savings of Tennessee or Washington state. What it delivers instead is a rare combination on this list: a large metro, a deep and varied job market, and home prices that have not caught up to either one. Huntsville, Alabama pairs rocket industry wages with below-average home costs Credit: Alex Blizky / Pexels Huntsville combines one of the country's highest concentrations of aerospace and defense jobs with home prices that still sit below the national median, though that gap is narrowing fast. Redfin recorded a median sale price near $350,000 for the three months ending in May 2026, about 17% below the national average, with overall cost of living around 9% below average. The city's nickname, Rocket City, comes from Redstone Arsenal, the U.S. Army aviation and missile command, and NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, both based in Huntsville. Cummings Research Park, one of the largest research parks in the country, has added a steady stream of aerospace, defense and technology employers around those two anchors. That combination has pushed median household income to $76,366, according to a 2026 analysis from the real estate research firm Real Wealth. The same analysis gave Huntsville a Housing Affordability Index score of 100, meaning local wages have kept pace with local home prices. That balance is unusual for a fast-growing city. Huntsville International Airport set a passenger record in 2025 and has continued growing through 2026, a sign of the relocation and business activity flowing into the region. Builders have responded with the most new single-family lots approved since 2007, though permitting has not kept pace with tariff-driven material costs and tighter labor supply. The trade-off for remote workers is timing. Median prices rose 3.5% in the year through May 2026, faster than several other cities on this list, and local forecasts call for continued gains of 2% to 7% through 2027. Alabama also levies a state income tax, so there is no tax-free advantage here. For a remote worker who wants proximity to a booming, high-wage industry without paying San Francisco or Seattle prices, Huntsville still offers a rare middle ground, even if it is a narrower one than it was a few years ago. Chattanooga, Tennessee gives remote workers the nation's first gigabit fiber network Credit: Sarah Swainson / Unsplash Chattanooga was the first U.S. city to wire its entire footprint with gigabit fiber internet, a distinction that still shapes its pitch to remote workers more than a decade later. The municipal utility EPB built the network, and citywide gigabit access remains a rare guarantee in a metro of Chattanooga's size. Housing costs have stayed competitive even as the city's profile has risen. Redfin recorded a median sale price of $360,000 for the three months ending in June 2026, up 4.3% from a year earlier. Zillow's home value index shows a lower typical value of $322,295. Multiple local real estate analyses put Chattanooga's overall price level between 18% and 21% below the national average, with cost of living running 3% to 5% below the national figure as well. Tennessee charges no state income tax, a detail that matters more the higher a remote salary climbs. Major employers in the metro include Volkswagen, BlueCross BlueShield of Tennessee, Amazon $AMZN, EPB and two large hospital systems, CHI Memorial and Erlanger Health System. That mix gives the local economy a base beyond tourism and remote transplants. Chattanooga's downtown sits along the Tennessee River, with Lookout Mountain and Signal Mountain both a short drive away for hiking, climbing and mountain biking. Buyers who purchased in Chattanooga in 2021 and 2022, when it was still a lesser-known relocation option, have done well since. One local brokerage's analysis put their gains at 25% to 35%. That appreciation is a reminder that Chattanooga's value case has shifted over the past few years, from an undiscovered bargain to an established, still-affordable second-tier market. For a remote worker moving now, the fiber network, tax advantage and diversified job base remain intact, even if the rock-bottom prices of a few years ago are gone. Knoxville, Tennessee pairs national lab jobs with Smoky Mountains access Credit: Joshua Woroniecki / Pexels Knoxville offers a similar tax and cost advantage to Chattanooga, its neighbor two hours up Interstate 75, with a different economic anchor: federally funded research. Oak Ridge National Laboratory, about 25 miles west of downtown, employs thousands in nuclear research, supercomputing and advanced manufacturing. Its presence has pulled in contractors and spinoff companies across the metro. Redfin recorded a median sale price of $325,000 for the three months ending in June 2026, up 1.7% from a year earlier. That figure sits about 19% below the national average, and Redfin puts Knoxville's overall cost of living 14% below the national figure. Zillow's home value index shows a higher typical value of about $374,000, a gap that reflects how much these two data sources weigh different segments of the market. Prices vary sharply by neighborhood. Downtown Knoxville condos and homes have climbed well above the metro median, with a recent median sale price near $625,000 in the urban core. The affordability case for Knoxville rests mainly in its suburbs and surrounding county, not its center, so remote workers chasing the lowest prices should expect a short commute from downtown rather than a downtown address itself. Tennessee's lack of a state income tax applies here just as it does in Chattanooga, and the University of Tennessee adds a steady base of university jobs and young renters and buyers to the local market. Knoxville also sits closer than any other city on this list to Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the most-visited national park in the country. That makes it a short drive for anyone who wants weekend access to hiking and mountain scenery, without living in a resort town. Migration into Knoxville has slowed from its pandemic-era peak, with inflows from California and Illinois easing over the past year. Local forecasters still expect modest price gains of 3% to 5% through the rest of 2026. That keeps Knoxville a solid, if now well-known, option for a remote worker who wants research-driven jobs nearby without paying research-hub prices. Greenville, South Carolina turns manufacturing growth into home equity Credit: Canva Images Greenville anchors one of the fastest-growing manufacturing corridors in the Southeast, and its housing costs still trail many comparable metros, as long as buyers look beyond downtown itself. Zillow's home value index put the typical home in Greenville County at $340,295 in mid-2026, and Redfin recorded a median sale price of $368,000 for the three months ending in May. Those county-level figures tell a different story than the city center. Homes within Greenville's city limits have sold for a median price above $500,000 in recent months, driven by demand for walkable neighborhoods near downtown. Suburbs including Taylors, Greer and Simpsonville sit well below that figure and are where most of the county's actual home sales happen. The regional economy has drawn steady investment for three decades, anchored by a major BMW manufacturing plant in neighboring Spartanburg County. A growing base of suppliers and advanced manufacturers has built up around it. South Carolina posted the third-highest net inflow of any state among Redfin.com home searchers in the first quarter of 2026, trailing only Florida and Arizona. Outdoor infrastructure has kept pace with the growth. The Swamp Rabbit Trail, a paved path connecting Travelers $TRV Rest to downtown Greenville, has become a selling point for remote workers who want daily exercise built into their commute to a home office. Greenville County Schools also operates one of the larger public school systems in the state, a factor for remote workers relocating with children. Mortgage rates hovering near 6.3% in mid-2026, combined with rising inventory, have shifted some negotiating power back to buyers after several years of a tight seller's market. For a remote worker comparing Greenville with pricier Southeast metros such as Charlotte or Nashville, the county's broader housing stock still offers a meaningful discount. That discount holds as long as the search extends past the most in-demand downtown blocks. Tucson, Arizona homes cost $100,000 less than Phoenix Credit: Canva Images Tucson gives remote workers most of Arizona's climate and job growth at a steep discount to its larger neighbor. Recent data puts Tucson's median home price between $325,000 and $365,000, depending on the source and month, against roughly $445,000 to $450,000 in Phoenix. That gap of well over $100,000 has held steady even as both markets have cooled from their pandemic-era peaks. One cost-of-living comparison from a pair of Arizona real estate agents found housing costs run 26% to 35% lower in Tucson than in Phoenix. Local salaries, by comparison, run only 4% to 21% lower depending on the field. For a remote worker whose income does not depend on a Tucson-based employer, that math favors Tucson clearly: a comparable salary buys meaningfully more house. The University of Arizona anchors the local economy alongside a long-established aerospace and defense sector, including major operations tied to missile systems and avionics manufacturing. That base has kept Tucson's job market more diverse than a typical retirement or tourism destination, even though it draws plenty of both. Arizona posted the second-highest net inflow of any state among Redfin.com home searchers in the first quarter of 2026, trailing only Florida. Tucson's climate cuts both ways. Summers are extreme, though slightly milder than Phoenix, and solar installation costs tend to run lower here, which offsets some of the electricity load from air conditioning. Winters, by contrast, are mild and sunny, drawing a steady stream of seasonal residents who put additional demand on the housing market between November and March. For remote workers weighing Arizona against pricier West Coast metros, Tucson offers a rare middle path: lower prices than Phoenix and a genuine university-town culture. The Santa Catalina and Rincon mountains ring the city, turning desert scenery into a daily backdrop rather than an occasional weekend trip. Spokane, Washington offers Pacific Northwest living at half the Seattle price Credit: William Jacobs / Pexels Spokane gives remote workers access to Washington state's no-income-tax status and Pacific Northwest scenery at roughly half the price of Seattle, on the other side of the Cascade Mountains. Redfin puts Spokane's median sale price about 12% below the national average, with overall cost of living about 3% below average. Actual price figures vary by source and month, generally ranging from about $390,000 to $450,000. The spread depends on whether the data reflects median sale price, listing price or Zillow's home value index. Seattle, by contrast, has a median home price above $850,000 as of mid-2026, and the broader Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metro area is not far behind. Even at the higher end of Spokane's range, that is still less than half of what a comparable home costs in Seattle. Washington state charges no state income tax, an advantage Spokane shares with Seattle but not with most other cities on this list. For a remote worker paid from outside the state, that mix of no income tax and below-average prices is hard to match on the West Coast. Spokane's economy has grown beyond its historic base in agriculture and rail. Gonzaga University anchors the city's east side, and local health systems and a growing cluster of technology and manufacturing firms have added steady employment. The surrounding region offers lakes, ski resorts and hiking within a short drive, without the ferry lines and traffic that come with life in the Seattle metro area. The trade-off is job market depth. Spokane's local economy is a fraction of Seattle's. This city works best for remote workers whose income does not depend on finding local work if a client relationship ends. For anyone in that position, Spokane offers Pacific Northwest living, a real four-season climate and a tax structure that keeps more of a remote paycheck intact.

item.title: Dow falls after payrolls smash expectations, stoking rate-hike fears
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.14
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell Friday after August's jobs report came in well above forecasts, pushing traders to raise their bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike later this month. Nonfarm payrolls grew 162,000 last month, far above the 53,000 economists expected, pushing fed funds futures traders to price in a 58% chance of a hike The economy added 162,000 jobs in August, dwarfing the 53,000 forecast by economists surveyed by Dow Jones. The unemployment rate remained at 4.1%, and prior readings for both June and July were revised higher. According to the CME $CME FedWatch tool, the probability of a rate hike at the Fed's Sept. 15–16 meeting has risen to 58%, up from 49.4% the previous day, as reflected in fed funds futures markets. The 2-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since January 2025 following the report. "An upside surprise in payrolls will likely ramp up concerns about a rate hike, but that outcome is in the hands of next week's inflation numbers," Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist at Morgan Stanley $MS Wealth Management, told CNBC. "If those come in cooler than expected, the Fed will likely feel comfortable discounting potentially inflationary signals coming out of the labor market." Despite Friday's decline, the Dow is set to close the week little changed. The S&P 500 looks poised to finish the period up about 0.4%, and the Nasdaq appears headed for a gain of roughly 0.8%. Markets painted a contrasting picture on Thursday, with all three major indexes closing higher after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would be "inclined" to support holding rates at their current target range of 3.5% to 3.75% at the September meeting. The Dow posted its best single-day gain since Aug. 4, according to CNBC. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: Walmart is recalling Great Value frozen berries in 16 states over E. coli risk
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.87
The recall covers one lot of Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend, an expansion of a broader outbreak investigation tied to a Chilean supplier The recall, announced September 2 by Chilean supplier Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A., covers 10-ounce bags of Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend containing strawberries, blackberries, and blueberries with UPC 7874211226, lot code 6040 01-6, and a best-if-used-by date of February 9, 2028. The affected product was shipped to Walmart stores in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, and Wisconsin, the FDA said. No illnesses have been linked to this specific product. The Great Value recall is an expansion of an ongoing FDA outbreak investigation that began with frozen blueberries sold at Publix under its GreenWise brand. As of September 3, the FDA and CDC had identified 17 people infected with the outbreak strain across two states, with illnesses beginning as early as May 11, 2026. Six people have been hospitalized and no deaths have been reported. Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. first recalled a single lot of frozen GreenWise organic blueberries on July 3. Publix then expanded that action on July 29, recalling all lots of GreenWise Organic Frozen Whole Blueberries and Whole Mixed Berries sold at its stores in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Virginia. E. coli O145 is a Shiga toxin-producing strain whose hallmark symptoms include intense abdominal cramping, vomiting, and diarrhea that is frequently bloody, the FDA said. While most otherwise healthy people will recover on their own, the infection poses greater danger to young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals, who are more vulnerable to hemolytic uremic syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition linked to kidney failure. Consumers who have the recalled Great Value product should keep it out of the food supply. It can be thrown away or brought back to any Walmart location for a full refund. Anyone who has eaten the recalled berries and develops signs of illness should seek guidance from a medical professional. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: Norway's sovereign wealth fund is proposing to slash its U.S. Treasury holdings
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.52
Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages Norway's $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, has proposed reducing the share of government bonds in its portfolio from 70% to 50%, a shift that would cut its U.S. Treasury holdings from 34.1% to 21.9% of its bond index.

item.title: CPSC warned consumers to stop using squishy bun toys sold on Amazon over deadly water bead hazard
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.36
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission warned consumers to stop using Ivyapingdianpu's Squishy Bun toys on Thursday, saying the toys violate the mandatory safety standard for products containing water beads and pose deadly ingestion, choking, and obstruction hazards.

item.title: Wendy's Halloween kids' meal is returning for a third year with 12 new toys
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.10
The seasonal kids' meal launches September 14 alongside the chain's returning Boo! Books fundraiser for the Dave Thomas Foundation for Adoption This year's collection includes six core characters and six variants — Numb Chuck, Sir Choc-O-Lot, E.A.T., Cold Foot, Shiver Wing, and Taranchilla — each packaged with a sticker sheet and mini trading card inside a themed meal bag, the company said. Wendy's Rewards members will also have a chance to obtain a 13th character through a drop in the Wendy's app, with details to be announced. The meal offers customers an entrée of two-piece chicken tenders, four-piece chicken nuggets, a hamburger, or a cheeseburger, paired with either Jr. Hot & Crispy Fries or Apple $AAPL Bites and a beverage, the company said. A book featuring the characters is also included for younger customers. Alongside the kids' meal, Wendy's Boo! Books coupon books are available now at participating U.S. restaurants, through the Wendy's app, at kiosks, and in bulk online through the Dave Thomas Foundation for Adoption. Priced at $1, each book contains coupons for five complimentary Jr. Frostys and a Kids' Meal for $1.99 with purchase. Ninety cents from every book sold benefits the Dave Thomas Foundation for Adoption, which works to find permanent homes for children in foster care, the company said. Canadian customers will gain access to both Boo! Books and six Frosty Frights collectibles at participating locations starting September 28, the company said. In Canada, all proceeds from each $3 coupon book go to the Dave Thomas Foundation for Adoption Canada. Both the kids' meal toys and coupon books are available for a limited time while supplies last. The Frosty Frights return comes as Wendy's has been leaning into limited-time collectible meal promotions. Earlier this summer, the chain partnered with Illumination on a Minions & Monsters promotion that included blind-box collectibles and a Banana Frosty Swirl tied to the animated film. That promotion launched against the backdrop of a 7.8% decline in U.S. same-restaurant sales in the company's most recent quarter, even as total revenue rose 3.3% to $540.6 million. item.title: Adobe is naming a longtime insider as its next CEO as AI rivals pressure its creative software business
item.description:

Adobe $ADBE named Anil Chakravarthy as its next president and chief executive officer on Thursday, tapping a six-year company insider to lead the software maker as it navigates intensifying competition from AI rivals. Chakravarthy will assume the role on December 1 and join Adobe's board of directors.

item.title: The 10 most streamed songs of all time on Spotify — and the stories behind them
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.63
The 10 most streamed songs of all time on Spotify — and the stories behind them The most streamed songs on Spotify of all time show how pop's biggest hits earned their staying power, from The Weeknd to Ed Sheeran A song needs about four billion plays to make Spotify $SPOT's all-time top 10 now, a number that would have sounded like a typo a decade ago. The most streamed songs on Spotify tell two different stories depending on how they got there. Some, like a synth-heavy Weeknd single or a Harry Styles lead single, hit that scale through pure, immediate saturation: radio play, playlists, and a release cycle built for maximum reach. Others got there the slow way, picking up more streams years after release than they did in their first month, revived by a TikTok trend, a Spider-Man movie, or a wedding season that never really ends. That mix is what makes this list useful beyond trivia. It is a rough map of how listening habits have actually changed since Spotify became the default way people hear new music. A 2012 alt-rock song about a fight in a car can now out-stream most of what topped the actual Billboard charts that year, because a platform most listeners had never opened yet turned it into an anthem for a very online generation eight years later. A ballad written by a Scottish singer nobody outside the U.K. had heard of can out-stream stadium tours, because grief and heartbreak translate across every market Spotify operates in without needing a single radio play. Streaming numbers shift daily, so any snapshot of this list is exactly that: a snapshot. The ranking below reflects Spotify's own count of all-time streams as of September 2026, and every song on it has already crossed four billion plays, a threshold that only a handful of releases per year manage to reach at all. What follows is not just the count next to each title. It is the writing session that almost got scrapped, the sample clearance that turned into a lawsuit, the movie placement nobody predicted would outlast the movie's own soundtrack sales. Those details explain why these 10 songs, out of the tens of millions available on the platform, are the ones that never stopped getting played. Blinding Lights by The Weeknd is Spotify's most streamed song ever Blinding Lights has been streamed more than 5.5 billion times on Spotify $SPOT, more than any other song on the platform. The Weeknd, born Abel Tesfaye, released it in November 2019 as the second single from his album After Hours, and it has not relinquished the top spot on Spotify's all-time chart since. Tesfaye wrote the song with Max Martin, one of pop's most successful songwriter-producers, and Oscar Holter, with additional production from Jason Quenneville and Ahmad Balshe. The track pulls from 1980s synth-pop, layering a driving bassline under Tesfaye's falsetto in a way that made it as recognizable on classic-rock-adjacent radio as on pop stations built for younger listeners. That crossover appeal is part of why it kept climbing charts built for entirely different audiences at once. Its Billboard Hot 100 run set records that will be difficult for any future song to break. Blinding Lights spent 90 weeks total on the chart, 57 of them inside the top 10 and 43 inside the top five, both all-time records. In 2021, Billboard named it the number one song in the Hot 100's entire history to that point, ahead of decades-old staples like Chubby Checker's The Twist. Part of the song's staying power on Spotify specifically comes from timing. It hit its commercial peak in the spring of 2020, just as much of the world went into pandemic lockdown and streaming became, for many people, the primary way they experienced new music at all. The song's retro, neon-lit music video and its steady use across workout and driving playlists have kept it circulating years after its initial chart run ended. The Weeknd has had other massive Spotify hits, including Starboy and The Hills, but none has come close to matching Blinding Lights' pace. Every song on this list has needed years to accumulate its stream count. Blinding Lights reached the billion-stream mark faster than nearly any song before it and has continued adding tens of millions of streams a month, six years after its release, a pace that keeps widening its lead over Shape of You in second place. Shape of You made Ed Sheeran give away songwriting credit Shape of You sits at number two on Spotify $SPOT's all-time list with more than 5 billion streams, trailing only Blinding Lights. Ed Sheeran released it in January 2017 as the lead single from his third album, ÷, pronounced Divide, and it became one of the biggest-selling songs of that year worldwide. Sheeran wrote the track with Steve Mac and Snow Patrol's Johnny McDaid, and he has said the song was not originally written for himself. He told BBC Radio 1 that the trio started writing it with Rihanna in mind, only switching the vocal to Sheeran partway through the session once the lyrics felt too specific to his own life to hand off. The song's melody drew comparisons to TLC's 1999 hit No Scrubs almost immediately after release, and Sheeran's team added No Scrubs writers Kandi Burruss, Tameka Cottle, and Kevin Briggs as co-writers on Shape of You rather than contest the claim. That decision followed a pattern for Sheeran, who had already faced separate copyright disputes over his earlier songs Photograph and Thinking Out Loud. A second copyright case reached the U.K. High Court in 2022, when musician Sami Chokri argued the song's central Oh, I hook was lifted from his own 2015 track Oh Why. After an 11-day trial, a judge ruled Sheeran had neither deliberately nor unconsciously copied Chokri's song, closing one of the most closely watched music copyright cases of the decade. Shape of You also spent 16 weeks atop Canada's national singles chart, a record that stood until Lil Nas X $TWTR's Old Town Road broke it two years later, and it reached number one in the U.K., the U.S., and across most of Europe and Australia. Its Caribbean-inflected production, built around a marimba riff, helped push tropical house textures further into mainstream pop long after the genre's initial wave had faded from radio. Sweater Weather by The Neighbourhood found new life on TikTok Sweater Weather has been streamed nearly 4.9 billion times on Spotify $SPOT, making it the third most streamed song in the platform's history, and almost none of that came in the year it was released. The Neighbourhood put the song out in March 2012 as the fourth track from their debut EP, I'm Sorry, and it later appeared on their 2013 album I Love You. Frontman Jesse Rutherford has said the song grew out of tension inside the band rather than a moment of inspiration. According to the group, the track took shape after members got into a heated argument during a car ride back from the studio, and that friction shaped both the song's mood and its writing session. On release, it performed respectably but unremarkably, peaking at number 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 in December 2013. The real turning point came seven years later. In mid-2020, TikTok users began using Sweater Weather as a kind of code, pairing the song with clips announcing their sexuality to friends and family, drawing on the lyric one love, two mouths, one love, one house. The trend turned the song into an anthem within LGBTQ+ communities on the app and sent its streaming numbers soaring; it gained more than 5 million on-demand streams in a single month that November, a career high at the time. That resurgence pushed Sweater Weather onto the Billboard Global 200 more than eight years after its original release, a chart debut most songs never get even once. Its official music video later crossed 1 billion views on YouTube, placing The Neighbourhood alongside a small group of artists to reach that milestone with a single clip. The band's original independent video was pulled after they signed to Columbia Records, meaning most of that YouTube audience has only ever seen the later, re-released version. Few songs demonstrate as clearly how a streaming platform can hand an older, mid-charting single a second life larger than its first. Starboy marked The Weeknd killing off his old persona on camera Starboy has racked up more than 4.7 billion streams on Spotify $SPOT, and its music video may be the most literal reinvention story in modern pop. The Weeknd released the song in September 2016 as the title track and lead single from his third studio album, featuring French electronic duo Daft Punk, and it became his third number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and Daft Punk's only chart-topper as credited artists. Where earlier Weeknd hits leaned entirely on his own vocals and songwriting team, Starboy paired his voice with Daft Punk's production, giving the track a colder, more mechanical low end than his previous album, Beauty Behind the Madness. The shift in sound matched a visible shift in image: Tesfaye had worn the same signature long, teased hairstyle throughout his early career, and Starboy's rollout was built around cutting it off. Directed by longtime collaborator Grant Singer, the music video opens with a masked figure suffocating a version of Tesfaye still wearing his old hair, then reveals the killer as a new version of Tesfaye with the short haircut that appeared on the Starboy album cover. The new persona goes on to smash trophies, platinum plaques, and photographs from Tesfaye's earlier career using a glowing cross, then drives off in a sports car with a black panther in the passenger seat. Critics and fans read the video as a metaphor for reinvention: Tesfaye was ending the version of himself that broke through with mixtapes like House of Balloons and signaling a more polished, pop-facing chapter. The strategy extended well beyond the singles chart. Starboy's parent album debuted at number one in multiple countries, and the title track's blend of Daft Punk's robotic disco and Tesfaye's R&B falsetto helped normalize electronic-pop crossovers that other major pop acts leaned into over the following several years. As It Was captures Harry Styles' pandemic isolation As It Was has been streamed more than 4.6 billion times on Spotify $SPOT, making it Harry Styles' most streamed song by a wide margin. Released in March 2022 as the lead single from his third album, Harry's House, the synth-pop track opens with a recording of Styles' goddaughter, Ruby Winston, saying, Come on, Harry, we want to say goodnight to you. Styles wrote the song with longtime collaborators Kid Harpoon, whose real name is Tom Hull, and Tyler Johnson, recording much of Harry's House in a home studio set up inside Sony $SONY Music Group chief executive Rob Stringer's house in Henley-on-Thames, England. Harry's House itself opened at number one on the Billboard 200 the week of its release in May 2022, giving Styles his second consecutive album to debut on top of that chart after 2019's Fine Line. In interviews, Styles described the song as being about metamorphosis and change rather than any single relationship, and pointed to his own experience of isolation during pandemic lockdowns as a source for its lyrics. The song's second verse, which imagines a phone call in which someone worries Styles is not doing well alone, reflects the nightly calls he had with his goddaughter during lockdown, the same calls that produced the opening voice clip. Musically, the track pairs an upbeat, 1980s-influenced tempo with lyrics about loneliness and disconnection, a contrast Styles has said was deliberate. As It Was earned Styles nominations for record of the year and song of the year at the 2023 Grammy Awards, though it won neither award; its parent album, Harry's House, won album of the year that same night, beating out heavily favored records from Beyoncé and Adele. On the Billboard Hot 100, the song spent 15 weeks at number one, the most of any song by a British artist in the chart's history, and it debuted directly at number one in April 2022, a feat only a small number of songs have managed. One Dance introduced Afrobeats sounds to Spotify's global audience One Dance has been streamed more than 4.4 billion times on Spotify $SPOT and once held the title of the most streamed song in the platform's history outright. Drake released it in April 2016 as a single from his fourth album, Views, featuring Nigerian singer Wizkid and British singer Kyla, and it topped the singles charts in 15 countries, including the U.S., the U.K., and Canada. The song's foundation is a sample of Kyla's 2008 U.K. funky track Do You Mind, specifically the Crazy Cousinz remix, whose vocal and keyboard stabs anchor most of One Dance's melody.
